# Next.js: How It Works

`vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/testing-library`, together with the plugin from `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/plugin`, runs a Next.js App Router app in the browser test runtime: the server that answers a request, the HTML it renders, and the client that hydrates it. This page explains how it works and what it does not do yet. The [Next.js guide](../nextjs-guide.md) shows how to use it.

It needs `next@16.4` or later. In that release Next's request stores became one per realm, which lets the three layers below run as separate module graphs. It also needs `@next/routing`, the Next.js package that finds a request's route, at the same version as `next`. See [The Server In Front Of The App](#the-server-in-front-of-the-app).

## The Idea: Port The Build, Run The Runtime

Next.js is two things. One is a build, written for webpack and Turbopack, that turns `app/` into bundles. The other is a runtime, in `next/dist`, that those bundles run on: the request handler, the renderer, the router and the caches.

Only the build is tied to a bundler. So this plugin does the build with Vite, and asks Next's own build code for everything that is not bundling:

| What                                         | Where it comes from                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| The app's routes                             | `next/dist/build/route-discovery`, `normalizeCatchAllRoutes()`                       |
| What the server does before a route          | `handleBuildComplete()`: what Next's build hands a deployment adapter                |
| Which route a request gets                   | `resolveRoutes()` from `@next/routing`, see [below](#the-server-in-front-of-the-app) |
| The request handler for `proxy.ts`           | `next-middleware-loader`, Next's webpack loader, called as-is                        |
| A route's loader tree: page, layouts, errors | `next-app-loader`, Next's webpack loader, called as-is                               |
| A page's request handler                     | `next/dist/build/templates/app-page-runtime`: `handler(req, res)`                    |
| A route handler's route module               | `next-app-loader` again, which expands `templates/app-route`                         |
| A route handler's request handler            | In the same template, `templates/app-route`: `handler(req, res)`                     |
| Compile-time constants                       | `getDefineEnv()`                                                                     |
| Module aliases, per layer                    | `createWebpackAliases()` and the other alias tables                                  |
| React                                        | The React that Next ships, through `createVendoredReactAliases()`                    |
| Compiling an app source file                 | Next's SWC transform, with `getLoaderSWCOptions()` for its layer                     |
| A call to a `next/font` function             | `next-font-loader` and Next's `css-loader`, called as-is                             |
| An imported image                            | `next-image-loader`, called as-is                                                    |
| A metadata file, like `icon.png`             | `next-metadata-image-loader` and `next-metadata-route-loader`, called as-is          |
| The plugins of PostCSS                       | `getPostCssPlugins()`, with Next's defaults                                          |
| The class name and the mode of a CSS module  | `getCssModuleLoader()`: its `getLocalIdent` and `mode`                               |
| An image behind `/_next/image`               | Next's image optimizer, `next/dist/server/image-optimizer`                           |

Everything behind those is Next's runtime, unchanged. What it writes to its server's response is the `Response` the browser gets.

The routes are listed the way `next build` lists its entries. Pages with the same pathname are one route, and a catch-all page in a slot is added to the routes it also matches. An app whose routes `next build` rejects is rejected here too, with Next's own errors: pages no route matches, slots that cannot render the same URLs, and, with `strictRouteMatching`, an interception route without the route it intercepts. The loader gets the options a build passes, so a layout with only slots has no `children`, as in a deployment.

### When Next Changes

All of this is internal to Next, and it changes between minor versions. The build code's output names the runtime it was made for: the constants the runtime reads, the files an alias leads to, the arguments a template passes. So the plugin does not bring its own copy of Next's build code. It calls the build code of the installed `next`, from one place: `project.ts` and the files in `project/`, which are typed against Next's own declarations. Every module of `next/dist` that the plugin names, in an import or in a string, is in `src/nextjs/compat/`, and a lint rule keeps static imports there. What stays outside is the layout of the package, not a module of it: `next/dist` against `next/dist/esm`, and `next/dist/compiled/`. In `compat/`, `compat/build.ts` loads the modules of Next's build that the plugin calls, and an export that is gone fails with the message below where it is read; `compat/checks.ts` has the checks of the runtime; the modules of `compat/rsc/`, `compat/ssr/`, `compat/server/` and `compat/browser/` are what the plugin's modules in each layer import of Next's runtime; `compat/paths.ts` has the paths the plugin names as strings; and `compat/patches.ts` has the edits the plugin makes to Next's own files, each with what does not work when a version of Next no longer has what it finds. What only production prerendering takes, `compat/rsc/prerender.ts`, loads and is pre-bundled only with `build: "production"`: `rsc.ts` imports it through a virtual module that is empty without it.

That code checks what the plugin relies on. It does so when a run starts, or for a loader when that loader is first used. The checks cover the build code, and the runtime that the plugin's own modules call in the browser. In the runtime it checks what would fail silently, or without saying why: a hook, a global, `document.currentScript`, what the `server-reference-info` shim replaces, the manifests. A static import of a name that is gone needs no check, because the module fails to link with a `SyntaxError` that names it. The check only reads the runtime's files and does not load them, because they run in the browser. A Next.js that differs stops the run with one message that gives the version and what is different.

| What is checked                                                                                                                       | Without the check                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Every file and export of the build code that is called                                                                                | A `TypeError` somewhere in the plugin                                              |
| `discoverRoutes()` returns `mappedAppPages`                                                                                           | An app without routes: every URL is a 404                                          |
| `@next/routing` is installed, at the same version as `next`                                                                           | Routes that Next's build hands out and its resolver does not read                  |
| `handleBuildComplete()` calls the adapter, without a build on disk, with every phase of the routes                                    | A `TypeError`, or a server that skips a phase                                      |
| The build has an output for every route, and `resolveRoutes()` finds it for a URL of that route                                       | Every URL is a 404, and nothing says why                                           |
| `getEdgeServerEntry()` loads the middleware with `next-middleware-loader`, whose template calls `require(`                            | A `require` that the browser does not have                                         |
| `getDefineEnv()` sets `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME` to `nodejs` for the server layers                                                    | Next's code takes another runtime's branches                                       |
| The alias tables have `react-server-dom-webpack/server$`                                                                              | A `TypeError` on a path                                                            |
| `IncrementalCache` takes `fs`, `serverDistDir` and `fetchCacheKeyPrefix`                                                              | Nothing is cached, or a test finds another test's entries                          |
| The SWC transform turns a call to a `next/font` function into an import of `next/font/.../target.css?`                                | A font function that throws, without a message                                     |
| The SWC transform marks a `"use client"` module in the `rsc` layer                                                                    | A client module that asks for the `require` of Next's bundler                      |
| `getNextFontLoader()` uses css-loader and next-font-loader, and css-loader makes a list of CSS with `locals`                          | A font without CSS, or without class names                                         |
| `getCssModuleLoader()` gives css-loader the `mode` and the `getLocalIdent` of a CSS module                                            | Class names and a mode of a CSS module that are not Next's                         |
| `next-image-loader` makes a module that starts with `export default {`                                                                | An imported image that is not what `next/image` takes                              |
| The app loader's output has `__webpack_require__` and imports `app-page-runtime`, which imports the route module as `module.compiled` | A `require` that the browser does not have, or a route module from the wrong layer |
| The `app-route` template loads `route.ts` with `userland: () => require(`                                                             | A `require` that the browser does not have                                         |
| `stream-ops` reads `process.env.__NEXT_USE_NODE_STREAMS`                                                                              | Next renders to Node.js streams, which a browser does not have                     |
| The app loader imports the module of a page by its file, by which Next's build finds the segments of a route                          | A page without its CSS                                                             |
| Next's renderer looks up the CSS of a segment in `entryCSSFiles` by its file without the extension, and links it under `/_next/`      | A page without its CSS, and nothing says why                                       |
| The client entry has `hydrate()`, which the plugin imports once the page is there                                                     | A `TypeError` when a page loads                                                    |
| Next's root component calls `__NEXT_HYDRATED_CB` under `process.env.__NEXT_TEST_MODE`                                                 | `renderServer()` waits for the page to hydrate until the test times out            |
| Next takes its asset prefix from the `/_next/` URL of `document.currentScript`                                                        | The app does not start in the browser                                              |
| `server-reference-info` has the functions the plugin replaces for Vite RSC's ids                                                      | Next rejects the ids of Vite RSC's Server Actions                                  |
| The route module reads the manifests through `load-manifest.external`                                                                 | Next looks for a build's files in `.next/`                                         |

A function that is still there but takes other arguments is not checked. A build-code function then fails with its own error at startup, and a runtime function fails when a test calls it. The check also cannot cover what Next's runtime does with these once a request comes in: a manifest field it starts to read, or a key it starts to require in the loader tree. That shows up as a failing test. For that reason CI runs the Next.js playgrounds against `next@latest` and `next@canary`, and every night `next-canary.yml` runs them against canary in both builds, then type-checks the plugin against canary's declarations, which shows a change of a signature before it breaks a run. A failure there opens an issue, or comments on the one that is open.

Next imports its Flight codec as `react-server-dom-webpack`. In the `rsc` layer that codec is Vite RSC's, through adapters that leave out Next's manifests. The layer has every export that the codec in the installed `next` has. An export that the plugin has no adapter for throws when it is called, and says so. A new export that nothing calls does not stop a run.

## Three Layers, Three Environments

Next compiles an App Router app into three layers. Each has its own module graph and its own build of React:

| Layer     | Runs                                                                            | React                | Vite environment |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ---------------- |
| `rsc`     | Server Components, Server Actions, route handlers, which requests are the app's | `react-server` build | `client`         |
| `ssr`     | Next's route module, the HTML renderer, the server in front of the app          | regular build        | `next_ssr`       |
| `browser` | Next's router, your Client Components                                           | regular build        | `react_client`   |

Here each layer is a Vite environment, with the aliases and constants Next gives that layer. All three run in the browser test runtime. That keeps the test white-box: the `db` your test seeds is the module instance the Server Component reads.

The `rsc` layer is the document's own module graph. The other two run in module runners: the `browser` layer has a runner for every page and one for the files with `"use client"` that `loadClientModule()` loads. The test, or another host, imports `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/testing-library`, the server's API, and the `rsc` and the `ssr` layer start to load as it evaluates. A host that renders only Client Components of its own files imports `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/client-components`, with `loadClientModule()`, which loads neither: the first page or request of the app does. In a static build the tab fetches the `browser` layer's file at once, which every page runs, from a `<link rel="preload">` in the HTML of the host's page, and the `ssr` layer's when that layer starts to load. Nothing that the host imports waits for the `ssr` layer: only a request that Next's server handles does. Which requests those are is decided in the `rsc` layer, with the build's routing alone, before the `ssr` layer has loaded; the `ssr` layer routes each request it handles again, with its own copy of the same module. See [Which Requests Are The App's](#which-requests-are-the-apps). Under Vitest the plugin's setup file waits for the `ssr` layer, so its first load is not a part of a test's timeout. Another host does not wait for it: the first request that Next's server handles does, which with a dev server includes compiling Next's server.

Vite's `resolve.alias` is one table for the three layers, and its entries go before Next's: an alias of `next/headers` to a mock applies to an import of `next/headers` in every layer, with a dev server and in a build. So does a resolver of the app's with `enforce: "pre"` that goes before `vitestPluginNext()`. Both replace a module of Next by the specifier the app imports it by: Next's own files import each other by a relative path, which an alias does not see.

A layer pre-bundles a dependency only under the name it resolves it to. An entry of `optimizeDeps.include`, the plugin's own, the app's or another plugin's, becomes the specifier of the layer: `react` is Next's React of that layer, pre-bundled once. With a dev server, Vite looks for a bare import that an alias matches among the pre-bundled dependencies, by the name it is imported by, before any plugin of the app resolves it. So an alias of `react` to itself changes nothing, where npm React under the name `react` would be a second React in the layer.

With a dev server a layer pre-bundles its dependencies once, before the first page: a dependency that Vite finds only as a page loads is pre-bundled again, which can load the page again. So each layer's scan starts where its module graph does. The `rsc` layer, the host's page, scans the entries of the host, the test files and setup files under Vitest, and the app's routes and proxy, which load only when they are requested. A host that names no `optimizeDeps.entries`, like a page of Vite's own dev server, gets Vite's default: the input of its build, or every HTML file. The `browser` and `ssr` layers scan the same files, the `ssr` layer none in `node_modules`, like Vitest's own runtime, which only the page runs: each loads the Client Components that a payload of the `rsc` layer names, by their id, of `app/`, outside it or of a package, which the scan reaches through the Server Components that render them. The `ssr` layer also scans the files of the `cacheHandler` and `cacheHandlers` of `next.config`, which it loads before the first request. Each scan reads a file of the app as Next's compiler gives it to the layer, so it does not look for the `styled-jsx/css` that the compiler takes out, and finds the `styled-jsx/style` that it puts in: Vite drops the whole scan of a layer for one import that it cannot resolve. A module that Next's compiler stops at in a layer, like a Server Component that uses `next/headers` in the `ssr` layer, it reads as it is. What only a module that the plugin makes imports, like `next/root-params` and the modules of the metadata files, the plugin adds to `optimizeDeps.include` of the layer. What a scan cannot find is a package of the host that the `browser` layer imports only from inside another package, which it pre-bundles with that import left to the page (see [Another Host Than Vitest](#another-host-than-vitest)): the page imports it in the `rsc` layer, as a module no file imports. A host lists such a package in `optimizeDeps.include`: only the host knows which of its packages are modules to pre-bundle, where another plugin of the host may resolve one itself. See [Another Host Than Vitest](#another-host-than-vitest).

Vite keeps the pre-bundles of a layer for as long as the hash of its config stays the same, and of the optimizer's plugins that hash has only the names, not what they resolve or compile. So the plugin adds two keys that no code reads to the `define` of each layer's optimizer: a hash of what the project gives those plugins, the alias tables of the layer in their order and the options of Next's transform for a dependency, and a hash of the contents of the plugin's own code, in `src` and in `dist`, whichever the package has. A change to either pre-bundles the layer again, without `--force`, and a run with no change keeps the pre-bundles.

Where Next's bundler config moves a module to another layer, the plugin does the same. The route module is created by the `rsc` layer but belongs to `ssr`. The route's request handler is in `rsc` too, next to the page, and makes the route module with the `ssr` layer's class. Client Components load once for `ssr`, to render HTML, and once for `browser`. A route handler is entirely in `rsc`: its `route.ts`, its route module and its request handler.

## Development Or Production

By default a test run and a dev server run Next's runtime and React with their development code, as `next dev` does. With `vitestPluginNext({ build: "production" })` they run them as `next start` does after `next build`: their production code, in all three layers. That is Next's router, renderer and request handler, and the copies of React, React DOM, the scheduler and the Flight codec that Next ships, which are the React of every layer. `vite build` builds the production code by default, and the development code with `build: "development"`: see [A Static Build](#a-static-build).

Next's files pick their code by `process.env.NODE_ENV`, and so do React's entry files, which then load `cjs/<name>.production.js` instead of `cjs/<name>.development.js`. So the plugin makes `process.env.NODE_ENV` the string `"production"` in each file of `next/dist` as Vite pre-bundles it (`build.ts`), and in the modules that Next's build generates for a route and for the proxy. It does so with a define of oxc, as a bundler does: a `process.env.NODE_ENV` in a string stays as it is, and so does one that Next's code assigns to. The JSX of the app and of the tests is compiled for production too, as `next build` compiles it: JSX compiled for development calls `jsxDEV()`, which React's production build does not have. A plugin that sets `development: true` for the JSX of `oxc` after this one wins, and then a component fails with a `TypeError` on `jsxDEV`.

In a test run the app's own `process.env.NODE_ENV` stays as it is, in its code and in its other packages. An app reads it for its own reasons, like secure cookies, which secrets it needs, or whether to send mail, and a test should not take the paths of a deployment there. A static build has no test and no dependency optimizer: there `process.env.NODE_ENV` is the build in every module of the three layers, the app's too, as it is after `next build`.

Production is faster. React's development build records where each element was created: an `Error` for its stack and a `console.createTask()`, for the first 10,000 elements of a render. A page is made of elements three times: as its Server Components render, as the HTML is rendered from their payload, and as it hydrates. And `<StrictMode>`, on unless `reactStrictMode` in `next.config` turns it off, renders a Client Component twice in the browser and runs its effects twice. In one app's suite of 1034 browser tests, most of which open a route, production took the suite from 51 to 41 seconds, and the median test that opens a page from 115 to 64 ms.

What a test loses in production:

| In development                                                                          | With `build: "production"`                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| React's warnings: keys, the rules of hooks, DOM nesting                                 | Not logged. A test that expects one fails                                                                                                                                   |
| React's error messages                                                                  | A number and a link: `Minified React error #418` is a hydration mismatch. [react.dev/errors](https://react.dev/errors/418) has the message                                  |
| The message of a server error in the browser, from a Server Component or from SSR       | The error has a `digest` and React's message `#441` or `#419`. Next logs the error with its message and the same `digest` on the server, so it is in the output of the test |
| Owner stacks, and what the RSC payload says of each element: who rendered it, and where | None                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `<StrictMode>`: a Client Component renders twice and its effects run twice              | Once. An impure render or an effect without cleanup goes unnoticed                                                                                                          |
| `act()` of React                                                                        | Not there. The plugin does not use it for a Next.js app. Testing Library's `render()` does, and throws. vitest-browser-react's resolves before React has rendered           |
| Next's development code: its checks and warnings, and `window.nd`                       | Not run                                                                                                                                                                     |

What changes: Next prefetches a `<Link>` as it comes into view, as in a deployment, also in a node. A prefetch is a request to the server, which handles one request at a time (see [Not Yet](#not-yet)). So a test that makes the data of a route wait, with a mock that returns a promise it resolves later, makes the prefetch of a link to that route wait too, and the navigation after it. Make the data wait once the prefetch has read it. The proxy runs for a prefetch too, as in a deployment, unless its matcher leaves prefetches out with `missing: [{ type: "header", key: "next-router-prefetch" }]`, as Next's docs show. The proxy cannot tell a prefetch itself: Next takes the router's headers off the request it gets.

What changes too: a page that `next build` prerenders is kept between requests, as `next start` keeps it, until `cleanup()` (see [Prerendered Pages](#prerendered-pages)). A test that changes the data behind such a page and requests it again gets the page of before, as in a deployment, unless it calls `revalidatePath()` or `revalidateTag()`, from a Server Action or a route handler, as the app would. A page that reads the request, or that has `dynamic = "force-dynamic"`, renders at every request, as in development.

What stays: a hydration mismatch, and what a Server Component or a Client Component throws, are reported as uncaught errors, which fail the test.

For a test run and a dev server the default is `"development"`. A test is where React's warnings are worth the most, and a test that fails is easiest to read with React's own message. A suite that opens many routes can run production on CI, and development where a failure is read:

```ts
vitestPluginNext({ build: process.env.CI ? "production" : "development" });
```

For `vite build` the default is `"production"`. A static build is a site that people look at, page by page, like the pages of a site that publishes them, where React's warnings go unread. In production a page of the e2e demo's build loads in about 60% of the time, with about 60% of the bytes, as `pnpm perf:static` measures it (see [docs/performance.md](performance.md#a-static-build-per-page-load)). `build: "development"` builds the development code, with React's warnings and messages and Next's checks, for a build to debug in.

This is experimental. CI runs the playgrounds with both, against the pinned Next.js and against `latest` and `canary`. The test of the e2e demo's static build builds it both ways, against the pinned Next.js. A run that switches from one to the other has Vite pre-bundle the dependencies again.

## The Compiler

Before Next bundles one of the app's source files, it compiles the file with its SWC transform, and with webpack loaders for fonts and images. The plugin runs those on the app's source files in each of the three layers, with the options Next's build gives that layer. Next's transform strips the TypeScript types, as in Next's build. Vite still compiles JSX and CSS. The exception is JSX in a `.js` file, which Vite does not accept: Next's transform compiles that too.

| What Next's build does                                                                                                                      | Here                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Checking what a layer may do: a client hook in a Server Component, `server-only` in a Client Component, `metadata` in a `"use client"` page | Next's SWC transform. The module throws Next's error when it loads, see below                                                                  |
| `next/font/google` and `next/font/local`, including when a package calls them, like `geist`                                                 | Next's SWC transform and font loaders                                                                                                          |
| `import logo from "./logo.png"`, including an SVG                                                                                           | Next's image loader: `{ src, width, height, blurDataURL }`                                                                                     |
| `next/image`                                                                                                                                | Next's runtime, and Next's image optimizer behind `/_next/image`                                                                               |
| `next/dynamic`, including with `ssr: false`                                                                                                 | Next's SWC transform, which leaves the import out of the server's code. `next/dynamic` also works without it                                   |
| styled-jsx                                                                                                                                  | Next's SWC transform, with the `styled-jsx` that Next depends on                                                                               |
| `compiler` in `next.config`: `removeConsole`, `reactRemoveProperties`, `styledComponents`, `relay`, and `experimental.swcPlugins`           | Passed to Next's SWC transform. Only `removeConsole` is tested                                                                                 |
| `"use client"`, `"use server"`                                                                                                              | Vite RSC                                                                                                                                       |
| `typeof window` in server code                                                                                                              | A define, see [Server Code In The Browser](#server-code-in-the-browser)                                                                        |
| `server-only`, `client-only`                                                                                                                | Next's SWC transform stops at the wrong one in a source file. In a package, Next's aliases make it a module that throws. That is not tested    |
| `paths` and `baseUrl` in `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json`                                                                                 | Read with Next's `loadJsConfig()`, and resolved for every app file, as Next's build does                                                       |
| Global CSS, CSS modules, PostCSS                                                                                                            | Vite bundles it, with Next's PostCSS plugins and Next's class names of a CSS module. Next's renderer links it, see [Stylesheets](#stylesheets) |
| `next/script`                                                                                                                               | Next's runtime, nothing to compile                                                                                                             |
| `require()` and `module.exports` in a source file, also next to `import`                                                                    | Compiled to an ES module, see **CommonJS** below                                                                                               |
| `next/root-params`                                                                                                                          | Next's loader writes it, with a function for each param of the root layouts of `app/`                                                          |

**Fonts.** A call like `Inter({ subsets: ["latin"] })` becomes an import of the font's CSS. Next's font loader writes that CSS: the `@font-face` rules, a fallback font with adjusted metrics, and the class names that the call returns. The font files are served under `/_next/static/media/`, where the CSS says they are. `next/font/google` downloads a font from Google Fonts when a run first loads it, as `next dev` does. Without a network it sets the fallback font and logs the download error. That is not tested. To keep a test run off the network, set `NEXT_FONT_GOOGLE_MOCKED_RESPONSES` to a file with Google Fonts' responses, which is how Next tests `next/font/google` itself. See `vitest.google-fonts.cjs` in this repository. Next preloads the font files of a segment, with a `<link rel="preload">`, or adds a `<link rel="preconnect">` where its fonts have `preload: false`, from a manifest of its build: which font files the module graph of each layout and page uses. Here that is read off the stylesheets of the segment, the same graph, as the route is requested. Next's flag in that manifest for a font with a fallback of adjusted metrics, for which it adds `<meta name="next-size-adjust">` to every page, is off: it is of every font of a build, and the fonts here are those of the routes requested so far.

**Metadata files.** A file like `favicon.ico`, `icon.png`, `opengraph-image.tsx`, `sitemap.ts`, `robots.txt` or `manifest.webmanifest` is a route of the app, by the path Next serves it at, like `/sitemap.xml`. Its route module and what a page puts in its head for it are Next's metadata loaders' own, as in Next's build: the data of an image with the hash of what is in it, `/icon.png?3c4d…`, the `.alt.txt` of an image, and the route of a file around the module that generates it, with `generateSitemaps` and `generateImageMetadata`.

**Images.** An imported image is the object `next/image` takes, with the file under `/_next/static/media/`. Next's image optimizer answers `/_next/image` in the Vitest process, as `next start` does, with the `images` settings from `next.config`, like `remotePatterns`. It keeps no cache, and tells the browser not to keep the image either. It needs `sharp`, which Next installs as an optional dependency. An image from another server is downloaded when the browser asks for it.

**Build errors.** Nothing is built up front. So the plugin finds an error that would stop `next build` when a test loads the module. The module then throws Next's error, as a module does in webpack's development build. In the `rsc` layer that fails the request, so `renderServer()` rejects with the error. In a Client Component it fails the render on the server and in the browser. Next shows its error page, and the error is logged and reported as uncaught, which fails the test run. A module that only a test file imports is also an `rsc`-layer module. If it calls a client hook without `"use client"`, it throws when the test imports it, unless it is in `browserModules`. What a test file with `"use client"` imports is of the `browser` layer, see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client).

An app source file is any JavaScript or TypeScript file that Vite serves and that is not in `node_modules`. A package is pre-bundled as it is, except for a file in it that names `next/font`. That file goes through Next's transform, as in Next's build, for a package like `geist`. The `rsc` layer shares its environment with the test, so there the test files, setup files and `browserModules` are not compiled. See [Server Code In The Browser](#server-code-in-the-browser).

**CommonJS.** Next's bundler takes a source file that calls `require()` next to its `import`s, like a page that reads a constant of `next/constants`, and a file of CommonJS alone, like a cache handler that `next.config` names with `require.resolve()`. Vite serves a source file as an ES module, where neither `require` nor `module` is defined. So the plugin compiles such a file of the app into one (`commonjs.ts`). A `require()` of a string is an `import` of that module, and returns what Node.js returns: the `module.exports` of a module of CommonJS, the namespace of an ES module. A file of CommonJS has `module.exports` as its default export, and the names that `cjs-module-lexer` finds in it, as Node.js gives them to an `import`. A `require()` of a JSON file or of a stylesheet returns what Vite has as the default export of it: the value of the JSON, the classes of a CSS module. The `import` runs before the module does, also where the `require()` is in a function that never runs. A `require()` in a `try` of a module that is not there throws when the call runs, so its `catch` runs, as with webpack. A `require()` of what is not a string, and a file that has `require` as a name of its own, are left as they are.

**CSS.** Next compiles CSS with webpack loaders: `css-loader` and `postcss-loader`. Part of what they do is bundling: they turn an `@import` and a `url()` into webpack requests, for webpack's module system to load. That part is Vite's here. What is Next's own, and not bundling, comes from Next's build code: the PostCSS plugins, as `getPostCssPlugins()` reads them from the app's config, or Next's defaults when there is none, and the class name of a CSS module, of `getCssModuleLocalIdent()`. A class `card` of `card.module.css` is `card_card__` and a hash, as Next's webpack build names it. Next's Turbopack build, the default of `next build` since Next 16, has a rule of its own: the plugin follows the webpack build, whose loaders it runs. For `next/font` Next's `css-loader` runs as it is, because a font's CSS has no `@import`, and no `url()` that it resolves. A PostCSS config that Next's webpack build does not read, but Turbopack does, like `postcss.config.ts`, is read by Vite. Next holds a CSS module to the mode of its rule, `pure`, where each selector has a class or an id of the module. Vite has no such mode, so Next's own check, `postcss-modules-local-by-default`, runs on a copy of each CSS module and Sass module, with the mode that Next's `getCssModuleLoader()` gives css-loader. A selector like `body {}` is then an error of that module, with Next's message, as under **Build errors** below, and the comment `/* cssmodules-pure-no-check */` lets it pass, as in Next. Sass needs the `sass` or `sass-embedded` package, as it does for Vite and for Next. `sassOptions` in `next.config` are Vite's options of Sass, as Next gives them to `sass-loader`: `additionalData` or `prependData`, and the options of Sass itself, with a path in `loadPaths` from the root of the project. Not `implementation`: Vite takes `sass-embedded` where it is installed, and `sass` otherwise. An `@import` with `layer()` keeps the order of the cascade layers that the stylesheet names: Vite inlines it with `postcss-import`, which puts an `@layer` statement after the imports before their CSS, so the plugin declares the layers of the imports at the top of such a stylesheet. A config of the CSS in the Vitest config, `css.postcss`, `css.modules`, `css.preprocessorOptions` or `css.transformer`, wins over Next's, and a run says so when it starts, as it does for `experimental.useLightningcss`, which Next would compile with.

### Stylesheets

Next's build lists the CSS of every layout, page and boundary: the CSS that the file imports, with that of the Client Components it imports. That list is `entryCSSFiles` in the client reference manifest. Next's renderer reads it for each segment of a route, and puts a `<link rel="stylesheet">` for each file next to the segment. So the CSS of a route belongs to its page. A page load starts without it, and Next's router adds the stylesheets of the route it navigates to, as in a browser.

Vite does it another way: a module that imports CSS puts it in a `<style>` when it first loads, and that is once for the browser. Global CSS of one route would then still apply after a test has opened another one. So for the CSS of the app the plugin does what Next's build does (`src/nextjs/styles.ts`):

- An import of CSS in the server code of the app and of its packages, in a file of the host, like a test file or a setup file, and any in the `ssr` and `browser` layers, gets a query, `?next-linked`. So does an import of a package that is a stylesheet, like `@fontsource/inter`. Its module puts nothing in the document, and exports the class names of a CSS module, as Vite's module for a server does: the plugin keeps the exports of Vite's module for the file, and drops the statements that add the `<style>`. A Vite whose exports need those statements stops the run with a message.
- Before Next renders a route, the browser asks the plugin for the list, over the websocket that the page fetches its modules over: every page load asks, and a request of HTTP takes a few times as long, longer still through a service worker of the app, like MSW's. Next reads the list before it loads the module of a segment. The files of the segments are those that the route's entry imports by an absolute path, as Next's build finds them. Next looks up the list of a segment by the name the loader tree has for its file, which is its path from the root of the project, without its extension: `app/layout` (see [A Static Build](#a-static-build)). The plugin walks Vite's module graphs from the file of each segment, in the `rsc` layer and, from a Client Component, in the `browser` layer. The graph has only what was loaded, so the plugin transforms what it walks first, which the browser asks for right after. It walks the modules of code only, as Vite tells them by their extension, and the page extensions of the app: not an image or a `.json`, and not a file that a module refers to with `new URL(…, import.meta.url)`, like the `.wasm` of a package, which Vite adds to the imports of the module. A Client Component in `node_modules` that is not pre-bundled has Vite's version of the dependencies in its id, `?v=1a2b3c4d`, while Vite RSC has its reference by the file, unless the page imports it by the name of its package: the walk looks it up by both.
- The dev server serves a stylesheet where Next links it: the path of the file under `/_next/static/css/`, or a hash for CSS that is no file, like that of a font. It is the CSS Vite makes of the file, so with PostCSS, Tailwind and the class names that its module exports. After the directory, the path has a hash of that CSS, `/_next/static/css/8d11792a12ffe139/app/styles/global.css`, as the name of a CSS file of Next's build has one, and the server says the browser can keep it, as `next start` does for `/_next/static/`. So the next page load does not fetch it again. An edit gives it another path. After an edit of a stylesheet without class names, of one that it `@import`s, or of a file that it depends on, the dev server tells the page the path of the version of now, and the page moves every link of the stylesheet to it, as Next's client moves its own links: a link of the new version comes next to each one, which goes once that has loaded or failed; one that has not loaded yet gets the new URL itself. The page stays, with its state. Every link, whatever its version: Next's development code puts the time of the request in the URL, `?v=`, so every render of the page with Next's router links it again, and React keeps the links before. Also the links of `linkStylesheetsOf()`, while a page has parked them too. Vite's client does not: it looks for a `<link>` of the module's own URL, which Next's path is not. The module of such a stylesheet in the code exports nothing and takes no update. An edit of a CSS module loads the page again, as its class names can change, and so does any edit with `experimental.inlineCss`, with which a page load has the CSS in a `<style>`, which is no link.
- With `experimental.inlineCss`, the list has the CSS of each file too, and Next puts it in a `<style>` of the page, as it does for `next start`. A navigation of Next's router still links it.
- `renderServer()` resolves once the stylesheets of the page have loaded, and the page is gone with them.

What differs from `next start`:

- **One stylesheet per CSS file**, in the order of the imports. Next's build joins the CSS of a segment into a chunk.
- **A node has the CSS of what its test file imports**, and of what the setup files import: the files of the host that render it, the default of `hostFiles` of `renderServer()`, which the plugin's setup file fills in. The plugin cannot tell which components a node renders. With `layouts: true` the layouts around it have their own. So does a component of a test file with `"use client"`, without a page: see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client).
- **CSS that a test file or a setup file imports itself**, with `"use client"` or without, is linked too, and is in the document while a use of the file holds it, as a page's is while the page is open. Every test uses the setup files and the test file: the plugin's setup file links their stylesheets for every test, also one without a node, see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client). A node has them, also one with `layouts: true`. A page does not: they step aside while a page is open, as the rest of the host's `<head>` does, see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server). With `isolate: false` those of a test file go once the next test file starts.
- **CSS that the host's runtime imports**, one of the `browserModules` or a package of the host, is Vite's `<style>`, which stays in the browser, as it would without Next, and in a static build the `<link>` of its chunk. A page switches it off while it is open. The CSS of a `next/font` call is linked all the same.
- **An edit to a CSS file** arrives with the next page load. A page that is open keeps the stylesheet it has.

[Not Yet](#not-yet) lists what Next's build does and the plugin does not.

## A Request

```
renderServer({ url: "/notes/1" })
  │  GET /notes/1                          the browser's fetch, with the app's cookies
  ▼
ssr      resolveRoutes()                   Next's route resolution: redirects, proxy.ts, rewrites
  │        └─ rsc: proxy(request)          the proxy of the app, if its matcher takes the request
  ▼
rsc      handler(req, res)                 Next's request handler for the route
  ▼
ssr      prepare(), render()               Next's route module
  │        └─ app-render
  ▼
rsc      Server Components → Flight        your page, layouts, data
  │
  ▼
ssr      Flight → HTML                     Next's own stream, with the Flight payload inlined
  │  200 text/html
  ▼
browser  the HTML goes into the document   once all of it has arrived
         Next's client entry hydrates it   in a module graph of its own, like a page load
```

After that, Next's router is in charge. A `<Link>` navigation is an RSC request to the same handler. A Server Action is a `POST` with a `Next-Action` header. Both go through the route resolution first. See [The Server In Front Of The App](#the-server-in-front-of-the-app).

## A Component

`renderServer(<Node />, { url })` renders one node the way Testing Library renders a component: in a `<div>` in `document.body`, without the app's layouts, and without the server in front of the app (see [Without The Server In Front](#without-the-server-in-front)). It is not a second renderer. The node is the page of a route, and the request for it is the one above.

```
renderServer(<Node />, { url: "/notes/7" })
  │  GET /notes/7                          the same request, with the app's cookies
  ▼
rsc      handler(req, res)                 the same request handler, for the route of the node
  ▼
rsc      loader tree → Flight              a tree with the node as its page, and no layout
  ▼
ssr      Flight → HTML                     no <html> or <body>: nothing in the tree renders them
  ▼
browser  the HTML goes into the container  with Next's inline scripts, which run
         Next's client entry hydrates it   the container, where it would hydrate the document
```

### The Route Of A Node

The route exists for as long as the node is there, at the pathname of `url`. The plugin writes its loader tree itself, instead of using `next-app-loader`. That loader reads a directory of files, and it ends the process for a page without a root layout. Next's renderer needs no layout. The tree goes into Next's own `app-page` template, with the injections `next-app-loader` makes. From there on the route is a page like any other, with the same request handler, manifests, cookies and cache.

For `/notes/7`, where the app has `app/notes/[id]/page.tsx`:

```js
[
  "(vitest-plugin-rsc)",
  {
    children: [
      "notes",
      {
        children: [
          "[id]",
          { children: ["__PAGE__", {}, { page: [loadTheNode, "vitest-plugin-rsc/component"] }] },
          {},
          null,
        ],
      },
      {},
      null,
    ],
  },
  { "global-error": [() => import("next/dist/client/components/builtin/global-error.js"), "…"] },
  null,
];
```

- **The segments** are those of the app's route for the URL, so Next finds the same params. Next's route resolution says which route that is, as it does for every request. By default it does so from the app's routes alone, for the URL as given. With `proxy: true` it goes through the proxy and `next.config` first, so a rewrite decides. A URL that matches no route gets the tree of `/`, which has no params. A route handler's pathname has a tree too.
- **The page name** matches the pathname, like `/notes/[id]/page`. Next derives the `revalidatePath()` tags from it.
- **No layout**, not even a pass-through one. So the HTML has no `<html>` or `<body>`, and it fits in a `<div>`.
- **Next's builtin boundaries** are the only other modules, and they sit at the root. They are `global-error`, without which Next's renderer throws, and `not-found`, `forbidden` and `unauthorized`. `next-app-loader` gives them to a root that has none of its own. They are Next's, not the app's.
- **The root segment is not `""`**, which is the root of every tree in the app. That is part of what makes leaving the node a page load, see below.

There is one such route for each of the app's pathnames, and one for `/`. They are in the same lists as the app's pages, and they load when they are first requested.

### A Node In The Layouts Of A Route

With `layouts: true` the node takes the place of one of the app's pages. `renderServer(<Node />, { url, layouts: true })` renders the app's route for that URL, with the node where its `page.tsx` would be. The entry is the one `next-app-loader` writes for that route. Its loader tree names the page by its file, and the plugin replaces that one module with the node:

```js
// what next-app-loader writes for app/notes/[id]/page.tsx
children: ["__PAGE__", {}, { page: [page8, "/…/app/notes/[id]/page.tsx"] }];
// what the route of the node has
children: ["__PAGE__", {}, { page: [__next_component__, "vitest-plugin-rsc/component"] }];
```

The rest of the tree is the app's: the layouts, `loading`, `error`, `not-found`, the slots of parallel routes, and the root segment. So the response is a whole document, with the root layout's `<html>` and `<body>`, and it loads like a page, not in a container. Both trees have the app's root layout, so a navigation to one of the app's pages stays on the client.

- The app must have a `page` file for the URL. A route handler, a path without a route and a route with only slots are errors, because there is no page for the node to stand in for.
- The page file is still a module of the entry, though nothing calls it. Its own exports, like `generateMetadata` and `revalidate`, are not used.
- The route keeps the app page's name, so the params and `revalidatePath()` work as they do for that page.
- The node owns its pathname while it is there, as a node without layouts does.

### Next's Router In A `<div>`

Next's client entry, `app-index.js`, builds the app and calls `hydrateRoot(document, …)`. There is no option for another root. The plugin already wraps `ReactDOMClient.hydrateRoot` and `createRoot` for the duration of that call, to keep hold of the root, which Next does not expose. For a node, the same wrapper passes the container where Next passes `document`. Nothing else differs. Next's own `hydrate()` creates the router state from the Flight payload in the page and renders its own `AppRouter`. So `Link`, `useRouter()`, `usePathname()`, `useParams()`, `useSearchParams()`, `router.refresh()` and Server Actions are Next's. No router state is made up.

The server's HTML is a fragment: hoisted tags like `<meta>`, the node, and Next's inline scripts. The HTML parser puts the leading tags in `<head>`, where React looks for them. What it puts in `<body>` goes in the container, in the same order: the node, with any `<script>` it renders itself, and after it Next's scripts, which run as they do for a page. The rest of the document stays the test's, so nothing is parked. The document gets a new `<body>` for as long as the node is there, holding what the test has in its body. What the node leaves on that body, like the listeners React adds for a portal, goes away with it. That is why the container has to be empty, and cannot be `<body>`.

Not every response for a node is that fragment. When it is not, the response loads as the page it is, in the document, and the container stays empty:

- A node that calls `redirect()` while it renders gets the page it redirects to. The node's route is gone.
- A node that throws, or calls `notFound()`, gets a whole document from Next, with `<html id="__next_error__">`. Next has no HTML for it and renders its global error page, or its not-found page, in the browser. Next's client entry does that with `createRoot(document)`, as it does for any page.

React listens for events on the root's container. For a node that is the `<div>`, not `document`. Only `selectionchange` is on the document. The plugin removes both sets of listeners when the node is left, as it does for a page, because the container can be the test's and outlive the node.

### Leaving The Node

A request belongs to the node when its pathname is the node's. A change of search params by Next's router, `router.refresh()` and a Server Action stay with the node. A navigation that loads a document is another thing, see below.

A navigation to another pathname gets the app's route for that pathname. Next's router then walks the tree it has and the tree it gets, from the root (`render-tree.js`). It loads the page, instead of navigating on the client, when three things hold at a segment:

1. The two trees do not match there. For the root, Next compares the segments themselves (`doesRouteStructureMatch()`), and these differ: `(vitest-plugin-rsc)` and `""`.
2. The new tree's segment is in its root layout or above it (`PrefetchHint.IsRootLayoutOrAbove`). The root of any of the app's trees is.
3. `isNavigatingToNewRootLayout()` says the root layout is a different one. It already does at the root, because the segments differ.

So the plugin's page load takes over, the same one a `location.assign()` gets: `document-loads.ts` stops the browser's, and `page.ts` loads the page. The node is unmounted, the document becomes the page's, and the node's route is gone.

This is how an app with two root layouts, in two route groups, moves between them. A node has no layout at all, so every segment of its tree counts as above the root layout, and none of the app's pages shares a root layout with it.

A link to the node's own pathname stays with the node. With the default URL that pathname is `/`, so a `<Link href="/">` in a node does not load the app's home page.

A navigation that loads a document loads what owns its URL. A reload is one, to the URL that is open. A navigation to the URL of the host's document goes to the browser as it is, like a host's `location.replace()` to it. Any other URL is the app's, and the plugin loads its page, as it does for a page the app navigates to without its router.

While a node is open, its URL stands in for the host's: any URL of the app's origin with the node's pathname. A node is the test's or the host's, and the app's route at its URL is another page, at `/` the app's home page. So a navigation to the node's URL leaves the node, which puts back the URL of the document, and lets the browser load the document again at that URL, without the search params of the navigation: `location.reload()`, `location.assign(location.href)`, a `<form method="get">` without an `action`, a plain `<a href="?page=2">`.

The URL says which it is: once the app has navigated from the node to another pathname, in the layouts of a route, the page there is the app's, and a reload loads that page.

Under Vitest a navigation to the node's URL loads the tab again, as a reload does without the plugin and in a test file with `"use client"`, and Vitest reports it as an error of the test file. In another host it loads the host's document again, at the URL of what it shows. The plugin cannot tell a reload of the app from one of the host, and does not have to. The page is left before a reload of the host's: the plugin leaves it before the reloads that Vite's client announces, at `vite:beforeFullReload` and `vite:ws:disconnect` (`document-loads.ts`), and another host leaves it with the cleanup of what it showed. So a reload with a page open is the app's.

In development a link in a node is not prefetched, and neither is one in a page, as in `next dev`. Next marks a link as visible only when `NODE_ENV` is `"production"` (`links.js`), and it does not prefetch a link that is not visible, not even on hover. With `build: "production"` it prefetches both: see [Development Or Production](#development-or-production).

### Rendering The Node Again

`rerender(ui)` on the result of `renderServer(<Node />)` renders `ui` in place of the node, without a page load, like Testing Library's `rerender`. The state of the Client Components in the node stays: a typed field, an open menu, a counter.

The node is a value in the registry, which the route of the node reads every time the server renders it (`loadComponent()` in `rsc.ts`). `rerender()` puts `ui` there, with the `wrapper` around it, and a new version, and has Next's router ask for the page again, as `router.refresh()` does: one request with `rsc: 1` to the node's pathname, with the headers and cookies of the page. React reconciles the new payload with the page. The server reads `ui` as it renders, so a render has the last one.

Every call is a request of its own. Next's router sends them one after the other, and React commits once the last has answered: a host that renders the node as a user types waits for one call before it makes the next, with the last `ui`.

It resolves on React's commit, once the effects of the node have run, not on the response. The server renders every node inside `NodeRendered` (`node-rendered.tsx`), a Client Component of the plugin that renders only its children, from the node's first render: wrapping it later would remount it. So the Flight payload of every node names that module, and the page loads it once. Its layout effect hands the page's router over once the node is mounted. Its passive effect, which runs after those of the node, says which version the page shows, and its cleanup that the node is not shown any more: a new version takes it down and up again in the same flush. Passive, because Suspense takes down the layout effects of what it hides behind a fallback. `node-on-page.ts` keeps the count, one per page of a node. Each page has a module graph of its own in the browser layer, so a page that was left tells its own, which nobody waits on.

| When                                                                                                   | `rerender()`                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The node still hydrates, behind a `loading.tsx`                                                        | Waits for it, then asks the router                                                                                                                                          |
| Two calls in a row                                                                                     | Two requests. Each call resolves once the page has its version or a later one                                                                                               |
| A Server Action, `router.refresh()` or a navigation to the node's pathname after it                    | Renders the last `ui`                                                                                                                                                       |
| The node throws, or calls `notFound()` or `redirect()`, as it renders again                            | Rejects with a `NodeReplacedError`: the page has something else there. The `cause` is the error React reported since the call, for `notFound()` and `redirect()` Next's own |
| The node threw before the page hydrated it                                                             | Rejects at once, without waiting                                                                                                                                            |
| A navigation of the app in the layouts of a route, or a Server Action that redirects away              | Rejects: the page has something else there, also while the node still hydrates                                                                                              |
| An error boundary in the node shows an error                                                           | Resolves: the node is still there                                                                                                                                           |
| In the layouts of a route, a layout or another slot throws before the node has hydrated                | Rejects: the plugin cannot tell that error from one in the node's place                                                                                                     |
| The app changes the history without a request while it waits: a hash link, `history.pushState()`, back | Next drops the refresh, and the node stays: it waits for the next call, or a request of the router                                                                          |
| `cleanup()`, `unmount()`, another `renderServer()`, a page load of the app while it waits              | Rejects with an `AbortError` that names what left the page. The request of the left page never settles: see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server)     |
| After the page was left, or something else took the node's place                                       | Rejects at once                                                                                                                                                             |

Something else is in the node's place when nothing has shown it for a microtask: Strict Mode takes an effect down and up again at once, and an error boundary inside the node leaves the node there. For a node that is not mounted yet, the root of the app says so: the plugin wraps its `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError`, which Next's entry passes, and any error React reports there while the node is not mounted means one took its place. In the layouts of a route that is also an error of a layout or of another slot, before the node has hydrated. For a node without layouts, a response that is a whole document, Next's error page, or one at another pathname, a redirect, says so before the page loads.

Only `ui` changes. `url`, `headers`, `proxy`, `layouts` and `hostFiles` are the page's: for others, call `renderServer()`, which opens another page. `renderServer({ url })` has no `rerender()`: a page of the app has no node to put another one in place of.

### What It Needs Of Next

Checked at startup, like the rest (see [When Next Changes](#when-next-changes)):

| What                                                                                                                                 | Without it                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The `app-page` template takes `tree`, `__next_app_require__` and `__next_app_load_chunk__`                                           | No route for a node                                                              |
| `next/dist/client/components/builtin/` has `global-error.js`, `not-found.js`, `forbidden.js` and `unauthorized.js`                   | No route for a node                                                              |
| `app-index.js` has `const appElement = document`, and calls `hydrateRoot(appElement` and `createRoot(appElement`                     | The node hydrates the document, or nothing                                       |
| `segment-cache/cache.js` compares the root segments of two trees                                                                     | A link from a node renders one of the app's pages in the container               |
| `render-tree.js` calls `doesRouteStructureMatch(`, reads `PrefetchHint.IsRootLayoutOrAbove` and calls `isNavigatingToNewRootLayout(` | The same                                                                         |
| `app-index.js` passes its root `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError`                                                                 | `rerender()` waits for a node that an error took the place of before it hydrated |

Not checked: the shape of a loader tree, `[segment, parallelRoutes, modules, staticSiblings]`. The tests that render a node fail when it changes.

## A Test File With `"use client"`

In React a file with `"use client"` is a client boundary: the file, and what it imports, is code of the `browser` layer. Here a test file with it is too, and so is a setup file with it. A test file with the directive is for a Client Component that gets only its props, like one of a design system, which the test renders as React does, with `render()` of vitest-browser-react or of Testing Library. A component that needs the app, its data or its router is for `renderServer()`, in a test file without the directive.

```
render(<Button onClick={vi.fn()} />)              in a test file with "use client"
  │
rsc      the reference module of the file          Vitest imports it, to collect the tests
  │  loadClientFile("/…/button.test.tsx")
  ▼
browser  the file, in one graph of the tab         with Next's React for the browser
         vitest, @vitest/*                         the page's own modules, not a copy
```

Vitest imports a test file in its own environment, which is the `rsc` layer, to collect its tests. There Vite RSC makes a file with `"use client"` a client reference, as it does every file with the directive: a module with a reference for each export, and none of the code of the file. In front of that module the plugin puts one line (`src/nextjs/client-files.ts`), which has the page evaluate the file in the `browser` layer before anything else of the module runs. The tests the file registers go to Vitest, since its `test()` is the page's own.

For a test file or a setup file, Vite RSC makes the reference after the plugins of the normal order compiled the file, among the plugins that are enforced last (`src/test-file-references.ts`): the reference is how the plugin loads the file, not a rule of the app. So a plugin of the test project sees the file as written in the `rsc` layer too, as in the `browser` layer, like Storybook's Vitest addon, which makes a story file a test file. A setup file that such a plugin adds in its own `configureVitest`, as the addon does in Browser Mode, is a setup file too. Not a file of another host, like a story of Storybook's builder: the reference module is the host's own module of the file, which the host compiles too, like the setup of its globals and its hot updates, so Vite RSC makes it where it makes the reference of a file of the app. The line in front of the reference comes after it, among the last plugins too, so `vitestPluginNext()` comes after `vitestPluginRSC()` in the plugins.

The line has the file's reference key, Vite RSC's name for it, and exports it as `__vitest_plugin_rsc_client_file__`, by which `loadClientModule()` tells the module and finds the file's evaluation (see [Another Host Than Vitest](#another-host-than-vitest)). A file of the app with the directive gets that export too, without the load. With a dev server that key is the file's URL in the `browser` layer, which the graph imports. A static build keys a reference by a hash of the file instead: see [A Static Build](#a-static-build). A file of the host can also be in `node_modules`, like a framework of the host that `host.files` matches and `optimizeDeps` excludes: a dev server gives the id of such a module Vite's version of the dependencies, `?v=1a2b3c4d`, and it is still the file. Any other query, like `?raw`, is another module of the file, and gets no line. The key of such a file is the URL of Vite RSC's module that imports it, so the graph evaluates the file itself once, as a package. A file of the project with the directive, a test file or a setup file, is evaluated once for each version of it, as the browser evaluates a module once: a second import of the file gets the first evaluation, and a change of the file, or of a module that it imports, evaluates it again. Every reader of the file has that one evaluation: the host with `loadClientModule()`, and a module that imports the file in the `browser` layer. That is the whole rule, and it is React's. Under Vitest the plugin's setup file has the graph forget the files before every test file, so Vitest evaluates them again for each, as it does the file itself: a setup file before every test file. A file without the directive gets no line: a test file without it renders with `renderServer()`, in a page with a graph of its own, and a setup file without it is server code, whose import of a file with the directive is a reference, which loads when something renders it. So the setup of the `browser` layer is a setup file with `"use client"`: what it imports, like a file that calls `i18n.init()`, loads once for the tab, as a module does. The tab is the page that Vitest runs the test files of a run in: a new one for every run, and with `isolate: true` one for every test file. List such a setup file in `setupFiles`; a setup file without the directive that imports it would load it once, without the hooks for every test file that Vitest gives a setup file.

The files are evaluated in one module graph of the `browser` layer, which lives as long as the tab (`src/nextjs/client-graph.ts`). What they import loads there once, as the modules of a test do without Next, and so does the library that renders. That graph is not a page's: every page that `renderServer()` opens has a graph of its own, and the two share no module. There is no request, no URL and no router of Next, and what a setup file set up in the graph of the tab is not in a page.

What a file imports from Vitest, like `vi`, `expect` and `vitest/browser`, is not a copy: it is the page's own module, which has the test that is running. The same goes for what another module of the graph imports from Vitest, like the `beforeEach()` that vitest-browser-react registers, and for `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/testing-library`. The plugin resolves such an import in the `browser` layer to a module of the page, which the layer's module runner takes from the page instead of fetching it. For the same reason the layer does not pre-bundle `vitest` or `@vitest/*` into a package that imports them. Every other import is the `browser` layer's, also another file of the host: what a client module imports is client code, as in React.

What else the plugin does for such a file:

- **After a change.** The graph outlives the pages. Before a file loads after a change, the graph evaluates again the modules that Vite invalidated for it: the changed file's, and the ones that import them, also through others. Any other module keeps its evaluation, also one whose evaluation failed for a reason outside its imports, as a browser does, and the graph keeps the packages, React among them. Watch mode runs a test file again when a module it imports changes: Vitest follows the importers of a changed file in the module graph of every environment, and in that of the `browser` layer the file imports it. Without Vitest, a dev server takes such a change to the module of the file in the `rsc` layer, which imports none of the file's code, so that the host imports the file again: see [Another Host Than Vitest](#another-host-than-vitest).
- **The browser's own APIs.** The file is outside any browser context of the app, as with Testing Library in Browser Mode: `fetch`, `document.cookie`, `cookieStore`, `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are the browser's, the origin's, which Vitest's UI shares, and nothing empties them between tests. A `fetch` goes to the network, so a route handler of the app does not answer it. See [A Browser Context](#a-browser-context). The plugin's setup file tells such a test file by the graph: it evaluated the file as one with the directive since the setup file ran.
- **Cleanup.** None of what a library rendered, as in Vitest without Next. The plugin's own `cleanup()` runs around every test, as for `renderServer()`: it leaves a page that is open. A library that renders keeps the roots it made, and unmounts them with its `cleanup()`. vitest-browser-react registers a `beforeEach()` for that when it loads, and in this graph it loads once, for the first test file of the tab, as Vitest loads a module that a setup file imports once per worker with `isolate: false`. So a setup file with `"use client"` calls `cleanup()` in a hook of its own, which is every test file's: see [Set Up](../use-client-test-files.md#set-up). The plugin knows no library that renders.
- **Stylesheets.** A file with the directive imports CSS with `?next-linked`, as a page does, its own import too, see [Stylesheets](#stylesheets). The plugin walks Vite's module graph of the `browser` layer from such a file, and links what it finds in the document while the file is used, as it does from a file of the host without the directive in the `rsc` layer. Every test uses the setup files and the test file: the plugin's setup file links theirs before the tests of the file, its `beforeAll()` hooks too, and again before every test, after `cleanup()` unlinked them. It forgets them for the next test file, which Vitest evaluates the files again for, also one whose tests are all skipped. A page of the app steps aside for them while it is open.
- **Errors.** What needs Next's app, or mocks a module, fails with a message that says what to do instead:
  - `renderServer()` rejects: client code cannot render server code.
  - A Server Action goes through `callServer()` of Vite RSC, which calls a global that each page of Next sets, to post to that page. While no page is open, the plugin has one there that throws: no page would answer, and the action would wait forever. It sets that one when the first file loads and when a page is left, never over the one of a page that is open.
  - `vi.mock()`, `vi.unmock()`, `vi.doMock()`, `vi.doUnmock()` and `vi.hoisted()` stop the run, see [Mocks](#mocks).
  - A link or a form that navigates, like Next's `<Link>`, which leaves the navigation to the browser without its router. The page would leave the test, and Vitest would lose the tab. The plugin's setup file keeps the tester's document with `keepHostDocument()` for the tests of such a file: it stops a navigation to another document, and reports an uncaught error that fails the run. Not a reload, not a navigation to the test's own URL, and not a link with `download`, which the browser downloads. A link to a route handler that answers with a file is not answered by the app here: test it in a test file without the directive.
- **Next's router.** The hooks of `next/navigation` are Next's, outside its app: `useRouter()` throws `invariant expected app router to be mounted`, and `usePathname()`, `useSearchParams()` and `useParams()` return `null`. The plugin leaves those as they are.

What the file imports is the `browser` layer's copy of a module. So a `db` it imports is not the one the Server Components read.

## Another Host Than Vitest

Vitest is a host of the plugin: it owns the Vite server, it says which files are its test files and setup files, and its packages, `vitest` and `@vitest/*`, are the page's own. Another host, like the builder of a component workshop, runs the plugin in a Vite server of its own and says the same with the `host` option:

```ts
vitestPluginNext({
  host: {
    // Glob patterns, relative to the project root: what a test file is to
    // Vitest. Not server code, and with "use client" a module of the browser layer.
    files: ["host/**", "src/**/*.demo.tsx"],
    // What `vitest` is to a test file: the page's own modules, also in the
    // browser layer. A name that ends in `/*` is every package of that scope.
    packages: ["host-kit/test", "host-kit/preview"],
  },
});
```

Both are facts only the host knows. A package of `host.packages` that the `browser` layer imports only from inside another package, the host also lists in `optimizeDeps.include`, so that the `rsc` layer pre-bundles it before the first page: see [Three Layers, Three Environments](#three-layers-three-environments).
