The plugin cannot read the packages off the files: a file of the host with `"use client"` imports `react` and `host-kit/test` the same way, and the first has to be the `browser` layer's React, where the second has to be the page's own module, whose spies the host shows. The same list keeps the host's runtime, and what it depends on, the browser's in the `rsc` layer, where every other package is server code. Not a package that the app lists in its `dependencies`, the same copy: that is the app's, server code, unless `host.packages` names it. A package of the host that depends on `next` or `react` would otherwise take the app's server along. A name can be a module of a package, like `host-kit/test`: that module is the page's own, and the package's other modules, like `host-kit/theming`, are each layer's, but the files of the whole package and what it depends on are the host's runtime in the `rsc` layer.

A file of the host can have an extension that is not JavaScript's, which a plugin of the host compiles to JavaScript before Vite RSC sees it, like `.mdx`: with `"use client"` at the top of that code, it is a file with the directive like any other.

Under Vitest the option adds to what Vitest's config says, and nothing else changes. The same mechanisms serve both, and without Vitest the host does what Vitest's config and the plugin's setup file do:

- The page imports `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/testing-library` itself, from a file of the host, and calls `renderServer()` and `cleanup()` itself: there is no hook to run them around a test. A page that renders only files of its own with `"use client"` imports `loadClientModule()` and `linkStylesheetsOf()` from `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/client-components` instead, which loads no layer of Next's server until a request of the app needs one.
- The host opens a browser context of the app for what it renders on the server, with `newBrowserContext()`, and closes it with `cleanup()`, as the plugin's setup file does around a test: see [A Browser Context](#a-browser-context). In between the page has cookies and a storage of its own, and the browser's stay the host's. A host that wants a page to start with items opens the context, then writes them, then opens the page, as a test does in a `beforeEach()`. `renderServer()`, `handleRequest()` and `runInServerAction()` open one when none is open, so a host that seeds nothing needs no call. Outside a context the document has the browser's own APIs, also for the host's code.
- A host that renders Client Components of its own outside a context, as React does, keeps its document with `keepHostDocument(report)` from `vitest-plugin-rsc/nextjs/client-components` while it renders them: without Next's router, a link or a form of a component would load another document in place of the host's. The navigation is stopped and `report` gets its URL; a declared download is the browser's. It returns what stops it.
- Leaving a page takes back every property that was set on the document, `<html>`, `<head>` and the container of a node while the page was open, and keeps what the host set there while no page was open, as before its first one. So a library that marks the document once, on its first use, is prepared by the host before its first page, and its mark stays for every page. `prepareDocument()` of `@testing-library/user-event` is one: it sets a symbol on `document` and adds capture listeners for `focus` and `blur`. Prepared while a page is open, the mark goes with the page, and the library prepares the document again on the next one, with two more listeners that stay: the plugin takes back no listener that a host adds.
- A host that stops a render, as it moves on to show something else, passes a `signal` to `renderServer()`. When it aborts, the page load ends and the page is left, as another `renderServer()` leaves it, also one that is still loading, and `renderServer()` rejects at once with the signal's reason, as `fetch` does: an `AbortError` unless the host gave another. Leaving goes on after that, and the next `renderServer()` or `cleanup()` waits for it. A render that has resolved keeps its page at a later abort, and an aborted signal opens nothing and leaves nothing.
- A host that shows the errors of a render reads `errors` of its result: what React reported on the root of the page, in order. That is a render that threw on the server or in the browser, an error that an error boundary caught, and a Server Action that threw into a form or a transition: the root that Next's entry creates says so to its `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError`, which the plugin wraps, as it does for `rerender()`. Not Next's own control flow, like a `redirect()` or a `notFound()`, which Next does not report either: the plugin asks Next's `unstable_rethrow()`. A render that fails still opens its page, with Next's error page or the app's `error.tsx`, so `renderServer()` resolves with the error in `errors`, as it resolved before for such a render; it rejects when there is no page to open, like a response that is not HTML. The array grows while the page is open, also with the pages that the app loads from it, until the host leaves it. An error that is not React's, like one of an event handler that nothing catches, is the window's, as in a browser.
- The stylesheets of a route and of a file of the host come from the dev server, over the websocket of the page, under Vitest too: see [Stylesheets](#stylesheets). A static build links them too, from `next-files.json` (see [A Static Build](#a-static-build)).
- A node has the stylesheets of the files of the host that render it, `hostFiles` of `renderServer()`: `host.files` says which files are the host's at all, `hostFiles` which of them render this node. A Vitest test never passes it: the plugin's setup file fills it in, with the setup files and the test file, which Vitest gives a `beforeAll` of a setup file. Another host passes the files of its own that render the node, absolute or from the project root without a leading slash: `renderServer(<Button />, { hostFiles: ["host/preview.tsx", "src/button.demo.tsx"] })`. Unlike `host`, what it passes replaces the default rather than adding to it, also under Vitest. A host that passes nothing, without Vitest, gets a node without the stylesheets of its files. A file that is not the host's is left out, with a warning: the CSS of a file of the app is its route's. In a static build the files of the host are what `host.files` matches, as there is no Vitest config.
- A host that uses the exports of a file of its own with `"use client"`, like a framework that renders a component of it, calls `loadClientModule()` with the module it imported. In the `rsc` layer that module is Vite RSC's client reference module, which has a reference for each export and none of the code, see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client). `loadClientModule(module)` resolves with the file's own exports from the `browser` layer: the evaluation that the module's line loaded. It links nothing. The file's stylesheets, those of what it imports in the `browser` layer, are in the document while the host uses the file: from `linkStylesheetsOf(files, { signal })`, which takes the files as `hostFiles` of `renderServer()` does, absolute or from the project root, links their stylesheets as they are now and resolves once they have loaded, until `signal` aborts, or without one until `cleanup()`, which ends every use. A document can have several uses at once, like the stories of a docs page, which end one by one: a stylesheet stays while a use holds it. A signal that aborts before the stylesheets load ends the use at once, and it rejects with the signal's reason, as `renderServer()` does; an aborted signal links nothing. A file without the directive gives the stylesheets of what it imports in the `rsc` layer, as for a node that it renders, like a preview of the host that imports CSS of its own: the CSS of every file of the host is in the document while a use of the file holds it, never as the file loads. CSS that the host's own page has whatever it shows, like the page's chrome, is the host's runtime: a module of `browserModules` or of a package of the host imports it, which stays Vite's `<style>`. A host calls it for a file that renders as it loads too. Loading a file is not using it: a host may load a file that it does not show yet, as it prepares what it shows next, and the CSS of that file is not the CSS of what it shows. While a page of the app is open, the stylesheets that were linked step aside; one that the host links during the page styles it, and leaving the page keeps it. It evaluates nothing itself, and it gives the same object for the same module every time, which a host that compares modules by identity needs. It tells such a module by the plugin's own export on it alone, so an export that a plugin of the host adds, like a list of the file's exports in their order, changes nothing. A module that re-exports such a file with `export *` has that export too, and comes back as that file. One that re-exports two such files with `export *` has two exports of that name, which conflict: a browser leaves the name out, a bundler may warn about it or take one of them. Give `loadClientModule()` the module of the file itself. The file is evaluated once for each version of it in the `browser` layer: a second import of the file, with no change of it or of what it imports between, is another module with the same exports. A new import of the file after such a change is a new module, whose line evaluated the file again: it gets that evaluation. A file that did not change keeps its evaluation, also when a file that imports it in the `browser` layer is evaluated again: the host's module of it and that file have the same exports, as a host needs that shows a file next to the files it imports. Any other module comes back as it is. It rejects for the reference module of a file that is not the host's, like a component of the app, since no line loaded that file: `host.files` says which files are the host's. The key in its message is Vite RSC's reference key, which in a static build is a hash of the file, not its path. A static build loads a file of the host with `"use client"` too, and a package of the host is the page's own there as well: see [A Static Build](#a-static-build).
- A host that says in its URL what it shows keeps the URL it moves to between pages: leaving a page or a node puts back the URL that the document had as it opened, not the one it loaded with. A URL that the host sets while a page or a node is open is the page's, and goes with it, as the app's own URL does: the plugin cannot tell it from a URL that Next's router sets. `?view=pages` of `playground/nextjs-host-demo` moves its URL between two pages, and while the second one is open. So a host that sets its URL before it leaves the page passes it to `cleanup({ url })`, which puts it in place of the one that leaving puts back: in the same entry of the history, with `replaceState()` as leaving does, and with the state that entry has.
- After a change of a module that a route or the middleware imports in the `rsc` layer, a dev server loads the host's document again. The page of the host has the modules of the `rsc` layer as the browser loaded them, the plugin's runtime among them, whose modules of the routes import the app, so Vite would take the change up through the runtime to the host. A host that takes such a change in place, like a framework that renders its own modules again, would then evaluate a second runtime next to the first. So the plugin has Vite load the document again instead, and leaves a page that is open first: the document and its URL are the host's again when it loads. That also goes for the app's CSS modules, whose class names can change, and its files with `"use client"`, which a route imports too, and for a module that both the host and a route import. Not for a stylesheet without class names, a stylesheet that it `@import`s, or a file that a stylesheet only depends on: a PostCSS plugin like Tailwind's makes every file it scans a dependency of its stylesheet, which then imports the file in Vite's graph. Its links move to the version of now (see [Stylesheets](#stylesheets)), or Vite swaps its `<style>`, and the page stays: what a page renders of the file is code that a route imports. The lists of the routes and of the middleware take a change of their entries for Vite's HMR, so that Vite's invalidation stops there and the runtime keeps its modules, for a host that imports them again after such a change. For a host it means that an edit of a component that a route imports loads its document again, also for a node that could have rendered again in place; a page needs the load, as the routes keep the modules they imported. A module that only a Client Component imports is not in that layer, see the next item. A change of another HTML page of the host keeps the page that is open, as Vite loads only the document of the changed file again. Under Vitest a change runs test files again instead, see [Watch Mode](#watch-mode). `test/after-a-change.test.ts` of `playground/nextjs-host-demo` changes a file of a copy of the app, also its stylesheet, one that the stylesheet `@import`s, and one that it depends on.
- A dev server that restarts, or that the host's document loses its connection to, has Vite's client load the document again once the server answers. With a page open that would be a reload of the page, at the page's URL, which the plugin would load again as the app's, in a document whose connection to the server is gone. So the plugin leaves the page as the connection goes: until the server answers the document shows the host without the page, and its URL is the host's again when it loads. Under Vitest the connection goes only as Vitest stops or restarts, after the last test has left its page. `test/after-a-change.test.ts` restarts the dev server of a copy.
- After a change of a module that a file of the host with `"use client"` imports in the `browser` layer, also through other modules, a dev server takes the change to the file's module in the `rsc` layer, which imports none of the file's code (`src/nextjs/client-files.ts`). The plugin reads that off the importers in the `browser` layer's module graph. Vite then tells the host that the file changed, as for a change of the file itself: a host that takes that change in place imports the file again, once, and `loadClientModule()` gives the new module's evaluation, which has what changed; a host that does not take it loads its document again. A change that also reaches a route still loads the document again, without the update. Not a stylesheet without class names, one that it `@import`s or a file that it depends on: its links move to the version of now, those of `linkStylesheetsOf()` too, and the host does not import the file again, so a host that does not take a change of the file keeps its document. A CSS module is a module like any other: a file of the host that imports it in the `browser` layer is imported again, as its class names can change. A host that renders the file again links its stylesheets again with `linkStylesheetsOf()`, which gives them as they are now, and ends the use of before once they have loaded, as `?view=in-place` does. Any other module that only a Client Component imports, the host sees as a page renders it again. `?view=in-place` of `playground/nextjs-host-demo` renders a component of such a file again, and `test/after-a-change.test.ts` changes what it imports, and a file that it imports, which the host reads itself too.
- `vitest` is an optional peer dependency, of any version. Only the setup files of the build import it, which the plugin registers with Vitest by their path, `nextjs/setup-browser.js` with Browser Mode and `nextjs/setup-node.js` without, and the chunk of what both run, which only they import. A host without Vitest does not load it. Under Vitest the plugin checks the version itself, and stops with a message for one older than 5.0.4.

`playground/nextjs-host-demo` is such a host: a page of Vite's own dev server, `index.html` and `host/main.tsx`, that renders a page of the app, a node in a container of its own, one node after another in the one document (`?view=switch`), a file of the host with `"use client"`, and a component of such a file that it renders itself with `loadClientModule()` (`?view=module`); a second page, `callout.html`, renders a node from a file of its own. Its tests start that server and drive it with Playwright, and its `build-test/` opens the same views in its static build (see [A Static Build](#a-static-build)).

`packages/storybook-nextjs-vite-rsc` in this repository is another such host, a framework of Storybook that runs the plugin with the `host` option: `playground/nextjs-host-demo/.storybook` is its project, and `test/storybook.test.ts` drives it.

## Route Handlers

An `app/**/route.ts` is a route like a page is, with a request handler from a different template:

```
handleRequest("/api/notes/1", { method: "PUT", body })     or fetch() in a Client Component
  │  PUT /api/notes/1                      with the app's cookies
  ▼
rsc      handler(req, res)                 Next's request handler for the route handler
           └─ AppRouteRouteModule          Next's route module: the request stores, cookies(),
              └─ PUT(request, { params })  redirect(), notFound(), HEAD and OPTIONS, 405
  │  200 application/json                  Set-Cookie goes into the app's cookies
  ▼
the caller gets the Response               its body as the handler writes it
```

There is no HTML to render, so the `ssr` layer plays no part. A module that `route.ts` imports is the same instance the test imports, and `vi.mock()` replaces it for both.

The request handler is Next's own, the one `next start` calls. It finds the route params in the URL, makes the `NextRequest`, and writes the handler's `Response` to the server's response. A handler that throws is answered with `500` and no body, and Next logs the error with `console.error`.

Next hands the work it does for a request after responding, like `after()` callbacks, to `waitUntil`. The request lasts until that work is done, so the callbacks read their own request's stores. A request that comes in meanwhile waits for that work, for one second at most. A nested one, which the server makes to itself while it handles another, lasts one second at most after its response. Leaving a page waits for all of it, also at the end of a test: five seconds at most, with a warning when it has to stop waiting.

## A Browser Context

The document has the app's cookies, storage, requests and navigations while a browser context of the app is open, from `newBrowserContext()` to `cleanup()`, like a new context of Playwright. Outside one, every API is the browser's own. A browser gives a page the cookie jar and the storage of its origin, which every other document of the origin shares, like Vitest's UI or a host's own, and the requests of a page go to the network. A page of the app has its own, as below, and its requests go to the app.

- **Who opens one.** The host, for what renders on the server: under Vitest the plugin's setup file, before the `beforeEach()` hooks of every test of a file without `"use client"`, and `cleanup()` after the test closes it. A test file with the directive is outside any, as with Testing Library: see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client). `renderServer()`, `handleRequest()` and `runInServerAction()` open one when none is open. A host's hook that runs before it opens one writes to the browser's own cookies and storage: under Vitest a `beforeAll()` and the top level of a test file, in Storybook a loader. A spy on `fetch` set there sits under the context's `fetch`, and sees only the requests that are not the app's.
- **What it has** (`src/nextjs/browser-context.ts`): `fetch`, which sends a request of the app to the app and every other one to the `fetch` that the document had before, see [Which Requests Are The App's](#which-requests-are-the-apps); `document.cookie`, a view of the app's cookies, see [Headers And Cookies](#headers-and-cookies); no `cookieStore`, `CookieStore` and `CookieChangeEvent`; `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` of its own, see [Web Storage](#web-storage); a navigation that would load the document loads the app's page instead, see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server); and `self.$RC`, which React's scripts of a streamed page call. Nothing of that is installed as a module evaluates.
- **Opening saves what the document has**, and closing puts it back where the context's own are still in place, with the same descriptors: the browser's `fetch`, the accessor of `document.cookie` on `Document.prototype`, the `Storage` objects of the window. A `fetch` of the host's that was there before, like MSW's, is what a request that is not the app's goes to, and is there again after. A patch that a test set over the context's own while it was open, like a spy on `fetch`, stays, also in the next context, and passes on to the context's. A patch that is restored once the context has closed, like a spy that `onTestFinished()` restores, puts the context's own back, which passes on to the browser's until the next `cleanup()` puts the browser's back: the plugin's setup file calls it before every test.
- **A reference that code took in a context** is the browser's after it: the context's `fetch` passes every request on to the one saved, `document.cookie`'s accessor to the browser's, and its `Storage` reads the browser's storage until the next context opens. So a library that a page loads, which takes `localStorage` as it loads, works in every context.
- **What a page leaves running**, like a persister or a listener for `focus`, uses the APIs that the document has when it runs: the browser's own after `cleanup()`, so its late writes land in the origin's storage, which stays. A timer that the page's code set does not fire once it is left, as a browser drops it with the page.

## Headers And Cookies

As in Next, `headers()` and `cookies()` are the request's. Next makes its request store, in `AsyncLocalStorage`, of the request it gets, here as on Node.js: the request store of a page, of a route handler, and of the proxy. The proxy and a route handler read the same request as `request.headers` and `request.cookies`. So the plugin keeps the headers and the cookies of the test in one store for the document (`page-store.ts`), and writes them on each request where it becomes one for the server (`sendRequest()` in `app-requests.ts`): a page load, a navigation, `router.refresh()`, a Server Action, a `fetch` of the page to the app, `handleRequest()` and `runInServerAction()`. The `Set-Cookie` headers of the response go back into the store, also those of every redirect it follows.

- **The headers** are the `headers` of what the test opened, under the ones a request sets itself, until the test opens something else.
- **`x-forwarded-host`, `x-forwarded-port` and `x-forwarded-proto`** are the ones of the URL of the request, as `next start` sets them for the proxy and the app, unless the request has its own. There is no `x-forwarded-for`: a request here comes from no address.
- **The cookies** are the app's, until the test ends. A `cookie` header in the `headers` of `renderServer()` sets its cookies in the store with the document, as a `Set-Cookie` of each without attributes would, so a script of the page reads them too. It adds to the cookies that are there, and they stay until the app changes them or the test ends. To change or delete one cookie in the middle of a test, do what a Server Action would: `runInServerAction(async () => (await cookies()).delete("session"))`.
- **A `cookie` header of one request**, of `handleRequest()` or `runInServerAction()`, is sent instead of the store's cookies, with that request and the redirects `handleRequest()` follows, not with the requests after it. On a redirect it has the cookies the response set, as Next sends the cookies of a Server Action with the page it redirects to. The `Set-Cookie` headers of the responses go into the store all the same.
- **A `fetch` with `credentials: "omit"`** sends none of the cookies, and its response sets none.
- **A cookie is a name and a value**, as in Next's `RequestCookies` and `ResponseCookies`. A `Set-Cookie` sets the cookie of its name, and one with a `Max-Age` of 0 or less, or an `Expires` that has passed, deletes it. Its `Path`, `Domain`, `Secure` and `SameSite` do not count: every request here is for the app, at one origin, as if it were an `https:` one. The value stays as the server wrote it, and goes back that way. `HttpOnly` counts for the scripts of the page.
- **`document.cookie` is a view of the store**, as it is of the cookie jar in a browser. A script of the page reads the cookies that are not `HttpOnly`, and the cookie it writes there goes into the store, for the requests after it. Like the state that shadcn/ui's sidebar keeps. As in a browser, a script cannot write an `HttpOnly` cookie, nor change or delete one. The page has no `cookieStore`: the Cookie Store API is a view of the browser's own cookies. Code that uses it checks for it first, like Next's own.
- **The browser's own cookies are not the app's.** They are the cookies of the origin, which here is also the origin of Vitest's UI, of the manager document of another host, and of any other app on `localhost`, whatever its port. The app does not get them, and the plugin neither reads nor writes them. The browser would also drop a `Secure` cookie on an origin that is not `https:` or `localhost`.
- **A `fetch` of the page gets no `Set-Cookie` header**, as in a browser, where it is a forbidden response header. The store gets the cookies. `handleRequest()` keeps the header, for the test to assert on.

The store is a plain value, not one of the plugin's `AsyncLocalStorage`. That one carries the stores of a request across its `await`s while the server handles it, and not further (see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server)). What sends a request, like a click or a timer of the app, runs outside of it. The document has one page open at a time, in one browser context, so the store of the context is enough. The requests of a page that overlap, like a response that streams while a Server Action is sent, share it, as they share the cookies of a browser. A request takes the store once, when it starts, and writes the cookies it gets to that one. Every browser context has a store of its own, so a request that answers after its test does not set cookies for the next one.

A request that the server makes to itself, like the one for the page a Server Action redirects to, carries the headers it was given, cookies included, as the `fetch` of a server does. It has nothing of the store, and its `Set-Cookie` headers go nowhere. For the request of `runInServerAction()`, which shows no page, the server answers it with nothing, and Next sends the redirect alone.

## Web Storage

A browser gives a document one `localStorage` and one `sessionStorage` for its origin, which every other document of the origin shares: Vitest's UI, the manager document of another host, another page of the app next to this one. So, as with the cookies, the page has a storage of its own (`storage.ts`), and the plugin neither reads nor writes the browser's.

- **`localStorage` and `sessionStorage`** of the window are a `Storage` of the plugin's each while a browser context of the app is open, where a browser has them: see [A Browser Context](#a-browser-context). Each is one object for as long as the document lives, so a library that took it in a context, like one that a page loads, keeps working: what it reads is the context's of the moment, and outside a context the browser's. Code that took the browser's own outside a context, like a module of the host as it loaded, has the browser's in a page too.
- **Their items are the context's, until the test ends.** Every test of a file without `"use client"` is in a context of its own, with new, empty items. A `beforeEach()` writes the items a page starts with. A reload or a navigation in the test keeps them, as in a browser.
- **It is a `Storage`** to the app: `instanceof Storage`, the methods and `length`, and the items as properties, which `Object.keys()`, `JSON.stringify()` and `for…in` show and which setting or deleting a property changes. A name of `Storage`, like `key` or `setItem`, is an ordinary property, as in the browser, so a spy on `localStorage.setItem` sees the calls. The methods are on a prototype of the plugin's under `Storage.prototype`, whose own throw for a storage that is not the browser's.
- **A page hears the browser's `storage` events, which are about the host's storage, never its own.** Their `storageArea` is the browser's storage, and their key one of the host's.
- **The browser's DevTools and Playwright's `storageState()`** show the browser's storage, not the page's.

## The Server's Disk

A browser has no disk, so `node:fs` and `node:fs/promises` of the server code are a disk in memory: [memfs](https://github.com/streamich/memfs), the package's own `vitest-plugin-rsc/node/fs`, see `src/node/fs.ts` and `disk.ts`. Only the `rsc` and `ssr` layers have it; the `browser` layer has no `fs`, as in Next.

- **One disk for the server and the tests.** The two server layers and the test files share it: a test or a `beforeEach()` writes, with an `import fs from "node:fs"` of its own, the files that the server code reads, and reads what a Server Action wrote.
- **It is empty at the start of every test**, and of every story of a server component or page in Storybook. `cleanup()` empties it, where it closes the browser context of the app, and closes what watches a file of it, `fs.watch()` and `fs.watchFile()`. A file that a setup file or a `beforeAll()` wrote is gone before the test; a `beforeEach()` or the test itself writes it. In Storybook a story's `loaders` run before the renderer's `cleanup()`, so a story writes its files in its `beforeEach`.
- **It has what Node.js has to start with: `/tmp`**, which `os.tmpdir()` names, and nothing else. `process.cwd()` is `/`, so a relative path is from `/`. No file of the project is on it. Next's cache writes its entries under `/.next/<n>/`, the directory of the build of the `n`th test, see [Caching](#caching).
- **In a worker of Node.js** ([The Node Host](architecture.md#the-node-host)) `node:fs` is Node's own, and the disk is the machine's: nothing empties it, and `process.cwd()` is the worker's. The host has a directory of the worker's own for the server's files, `PageHost.serverDir` (`src/page-host.ts`), made as the first page asks for it in a directory of the run in the system's temporary directory, which Vitest's own process makes and removes as Vitest closes (`configureVitest` of `src/index.ts`): a worker that Vitest stops gets no `exit` to clean up in. Next's cache writes under `<serverDir>/.next/<n>/`, which a browser's host has as `/.next/<n>/`, with `serverDir` empty. A test's `.next/<n>` stays until the run ends; the next test has its own.
- **Only where it is imported**, as the other stand-ins of Node's modules are. A dependency that says what it uses for `fs` in a browser, in the `browser` field of its `package.json`, gets that from Vite, not the disk: PGlite has `false` for it. The app's own `browser` field is not one, as Next's server does not read it. In the build of the notes demo nothing else imports `fs`, so memfs is not in it.

## The Server In Front Of The App

Before a route gets a request, a server has decided which route that is. In a deployment that server is `next start`, or the platform the app is deployed to. It applies the `redirects`, `headers` and `rewrites` from `next.config`, redirects a URL with a trailing slash, runs `proxy.ts`, and then looks for the route. Here that server runs in the browser too, in front of the request handlers above.

Next has a contract for a platform that does this itself: a deployment adapter. `next build` hands an adapter that server's routes, in the order they apply, and what it built for each pathname. Next ships the matching resolution as a separate package, `@next/routing`. The plugin is such an adapter:

| What                                                           | Where it comes from                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The redirects, rewrites and headers from `next.config`         | `loadCustomRoutes()`, which adds Next's own trailing-slash redirect                                         |
| An interception route, which is a rewrite to Next              | `generateInterceptionRoutesRewrites()`                                                                      |
| A build's routes manifest, which Next's route module reads too | `generateRoutesManifest()`                                                                                  |
| The proxy's file and its matcher                               | `getFilesInDir()` with Next's names for the file, `createPagesMapping()`, `getStaticInfoIncludingLayouts()` |
| The server's routes, in their phases, and the outputs          | `handleBuildComplete()`, which calls the adapter's `onBuildComplete()` in `adapter.ts`                      |
| The headers that a request may not bring                       | `filterInternalHeaders()`, which `next start` calls on every request                                        |
| Which route a request gets, a redirect, or a rewrite           | `resolveRoutes()` from `@next/routing`, in the browser                                                      |
| The proxy's request handler                                    | `getEdgeServerEntry()` and `next-middleware-loader`, which expands `templates/middleware`                   |
| What the proxy's response means for the request                | `responseToMiddlewareResult()` from `@next/routing`                                                         |

An interception route, like `@modal/(.)photo/[id]`, needs no plugin code for this. Next's build turns it into a rewrite, for a router request that says which page it comes from.

`handleBuildComplete()` is the end of `next build`. It runs here without a build. It gets the manifests of a build whose routes read no files, and an empty directory for the rest. The dynamic routes' patterns, the conversion of a redirect to a `Location` header and the proxy's matcher are what Next computes for an adapter. The plugin writes the manifests that Next computes them from: a function for each route, and for a proxy without its own matcher the matcher for every path, as Next's build writes it.

Two `next.config` settings are left out. `i18n` belongs to the Pages Router, and the plugin drops it from the config altogether. An App Router URL has no locale, and with `i18n` set the resolution and the proxy look for one in every URL. `output: "export"` is left out for this step, because with it Next's build reads the files it exported. The app's routes are the same without them.

### `@next/routing`

`resolveRoutes()` takes a URL, the request headers, the routes and the outputs' pathnames, and says what the request becomes: a redirect, a rewrite to another server, a response from the proxy, or a route with its params. It uses only web APIs and has no dependencies, so it runs in the browser unchanged. Its phases, in order:

```
beforeMiddleware    the headers and the redirects of next.config, the trailing slash
proxy.ts            if its matcher takes the request
beforeFiles         rewrites, also at a URL that a route has
the outputs         the routes with a fixed path
afterFiles          rewrites
dynamicRoutes       the routes with a dynamic segment
fallback            rewrites, for a URL that no route has
```

The routes also have `onMatch`, which is not a phase of its own: it holds headers that the resolution adds once it has found a route.

This is the server of a deployment through an adapter, which is not `next start` in every detail. A test pins two differences. First, `resolveRoutes()` also runs the proxy for a request that `next.config` redirects, or whose trailing slash is redirected, and answers with the redirect afterwards. `next start` answers with the redirect first. Second, it matches a URL against a dynamic route's pattern in any letter case. `/Docs/Routing` is the route `/docs/[slug]` with `Routing` as the slug, where `next start` has no route for it.

`@next/routing` is a separate package: a project installs it alongside `next`, at the same version. The two are released together, and what one version of Next hands an adapter is what that version of the package reads. The adapter API has been stable since Next.js 16.2. But what it hands an adapter has no version of its own and grows from release to release: between 16.2 and 16.4 it gained the proxy's matchers. So the plugin does not accept another version as close enough. A run stops when the versions differ, or when the package is missing, and names the version to install. At startup the plugin also resolves a URL for every route in the app, with the routes it got. A build and a resolver that no longer fit would make every URL a 404.

### What The Adapter Does Itself

`@next/routing` finds the route. What happens next is up to the adapter, and Next's own adapters have code for each of these too. Here that code is in `handle()` in `ssr.ts`:

- **Next's internal headers** are taken off a request when it comes in, before the resolution and the proxy read it. These are the headers that only Next's own layers set on a request, like `x-middleware-set-cookie`. A request that brought one itself would have a cookie that the app never set. The proxy sets them on the request afterwards, for the route.
- **A redirect** is a response with the status and the headers the resolution gives.
- **A response of the proxy with a `Location` header** and a status that is no redirect is the answer to the request, with its body, as `next start` answers it. `responseToMiddlewareResult()` of `@next/routing` keeps such a header for the response and sends the request on to a route, so the adapter reads that case itself: see `middlewareResult()` in `server-in-front.ts`.
- **A rewrite to another server** is a `fetch` to that server, where `next start` proxies the request. The browser makes the request, so its rules for a request apply: CORS applies, a redirect is followed, and the browser sets the request's `host`, `cookie` and `origin`. The app's cookies do not go with it. A destination on the app's own origin is answered by the dev server, not by the app.
- **A route** is called with the URL the browser asked for, even after a rewrite, as `next start` calls it. So `usePathname()` says where the browser is, not where the rewrite went. The route gets the rest through the request meta, where `next start` and a deployment adapter put it. The request meta carries the route's params. They come from the pathname the resolution ends at, read with Next's own matcher for the route. They do not come from the resolution's query, which also has them under names like `nxtPid`, because `@next/routing` reads a `+` or a `%25` in them as a query does. After a rewrite, the request meta also carries the query of the rewrite's destination. A request that was not rewritten keeps the query of its URL.
- **`x-nextjs-rewritten-path` and `x-nextjs-rewritten-query`** are set for a request from Next's router that was rewritten. `next start` sets them for a `next.config` rewrite, and Next's own code sets them for a proxy rewrite. The query leaves out `_rsc`, which the router adds to its own requests.
- **The headers** that the resolution has for the response, from `next.config` and the proxy, are set on the response before the route runs, as `next start` does. A page adds to them, like React's `Link` for its stylesheets. A route handler cannot replace one: Next sets a header of its `Response` only where there is none, apart from `set-cookie`, `vary`, `www-authenticate` and `proxy-authenticate`, which it adds to. A cookie from either side is set. The resolution has no headers for a request that the proxy answers itself, so that response lacks the `next.config` headers, which `next start` does set.
- **How a request spells a pathname.** `resolveRoutes()` compares a pathname with the outputs exactly as it is written. So each output is also listed percent-encoded, the way a URL spells `/release notes`, and with `trailingSlash: true` also with the slash. Another spelling of the same path, like `%c3%bc` for `%C3%BC`, is not listed, although `next start` does find the route for it. A dynamic route is found by its pattern, which has the folders as they are named. So `resolveRoutes()` does not find a dynamic route under a folder whose name a URL percent-encodes, and a run warns about those routes when it starts.
- **A request that resolves to nothing** gets the not-found page, or goes to the network: see [below](#which-requests-are-the-apps). That includes a rewrite to a path that no route has, like a file in `public/`. The resolution does not say where such a rewrite went, so the network is asked for the request's URL.
- **The not-found page's status**, `404`, is set on the response before the route runs, as `next start` sets it. Next reads it while it renders, and adds `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`. The response keeps the status that Next's handler leaves. So a Server Action request for a path that no route has is answered for the action, with `400` or `409`.

### The Proxy

`proxy.ts`, called `middleware.ts` before Next.js 16, is a module in the `rsc` layer, which the test shares. So the proxy is the same instance the test imports, and so are the modules it imports, and `vi.mock()` replaces them for both. In a deployment it is a separate bundle.

Its request handler is Next's: the template that Next's build expands for it, around `adapter()`. `adapter()` makes the `NextRequest`, enters the request stores, and turns `NextResponse.next()`, `rewrite()` and `redirect()` into the headers the resolution reads. The handler takes a `Request` and answers with a `Response`, on Node.js too. For Node.js the template loads two modules with the `require` of Next's bundler, which is `import()` here.

The proxy finishes before the route starts, so it has its own scope for Next's request stores. Its `after()` callbacks run once it has returned, as in Next, and read its stores: the route waits for what the proxy hands to `waitUntil()`, for one second at most. See [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server). A proxy that throws is answered with `500`, and the error is logged with `console.error`. `next start` answers with its error page.

### Which Requests Are The App's

The app's origin is also the origin of the Vite dev server, which serves the test's modules and the app's. So the browser's `fetch` has to choose. A same-origin request goes to the Next.js server when:

- Next's router or a Server Action sent it, both of which mark their requests with a header, or
- the server has something for it: one of the app's routes, a redirect or a rewrite from `next.config`, or a proxy whose matcher takes it.

The server answers that question with its route resolution, without running anything. That answer is the document's: it is worked out in the `rsc` layer with the routes of the build and `@next/routing`, and needs no other layer, nor the proxy itself. So a request that is not the app's goes to the network at once, also before the `ssr` layer has loaded, and one that is waits for that layer, which handles it. As with `fetch`, a request whose signal aborted while it waited for the layer is not sent: the document of a page load that was left, as a host cleans up before what it shows next. Any other request that waited is sent, like one of the host's own that the proxy's matcher takes. A request of a page that was left is dropped by the server (see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server)). Only running the proxy tells what it does with a request, so a request that its matcher takes goes to the server. If the proxy lets the request through and no route has it, a deployment looks for a file. Here the request then goes to the network after all, which has the files in `public/`.

Everything else goes to the network right away: Vite's modules, files in `public/`, a service worker. A `blob:` URL has the document's origin, and is the document's own: the browser answers it. A page load always belongs to the app: `renderServer()`, `handleRequest()` and a navigation get the not-found page for a URL that resolves to nothing.

A `fetch` that the server makes to its own origin while it renders is chosen the same way, and goes through the proxy too. The server handles it right away, inside the request that waits for it, and follows a redirect, as a server's `fetch` does. Like Node's `fetch`, it rejects a URL that is only a path.

### Without The Server In Front

`proxy` says whether a test goes through this server. `renderServer({ url })` does by default, and `renderServer(<Node />, { url })` does not. With `proxy: false` the URL is taken as it is. `resolveRoutes()` then gets `routing.appRoutes`, which the plugin makes next to the routes when it loads the project: the same routes without `beforeMiddleware`, the proxy's matchers, `afterFiles` and `fallback`, and with only the interception routes of `beforeFiles`. What is left is Next's own: the outputs, `dynamicRoutes`, `onMatch` and the interception routes. So a pathname gets its route with the same params, no redirect, rewrite or header of `next.config` applies, the trailing-slash redirect included, and the proxy does not run.

That holds for the requests that belong to what the test opened, which are the ones to its pathname. `renderServer()` puts the pathname in the registry, with `proxy` and the node, if there is one. `handle()` and `takesRequest()` look it up for every request. So the document, a Server Action, `router.refresh()`, a change of search params and a `handleRequest()` of the test all skip the server in front. So does a client-side navigation back to that pathname. A request to another pathname is the app's, and goes through it: a navigation to another route, a `fetch` to `/api/…`, a page a Server Action redirects to. The pathname goes with the document it opened: it is forgotten when the browser loads another page, also a reload of the same URL, and when the document request ends at another pathname, after a redirect from the page itself. `runInServerAction()` brings a route of its own for its one request instead, without the registry: a node that renders nothing, at the pathname of its URL. A page that is open keeps its own.

## What Stands In For A Server

The server layers run as Next's Node.js server does, with the web APIs that Node.js and a browser share: web streams, `fetch`, `crypto`. The plugin adds the rest of that platform. [The Node.js Runtime](#the-nodejs-runtime) covers what is Node's own.

- **`Request` and `Response`** that keep `Cookie` and `Set-Cookie`, which a browser drops from its own.
- **`fetch`**, so that Next patches the server's `fetch`, not the page's. Next patches it from the `rsc` layer when it first renders, and both server layers call the result. The server's `fetch` and the page's reach the same network.
- **`AsyncLocalStorage`**. A browser cannot carry a store across `await`. Requests are handled one at a time, and the store a request entered first stays readable until the request ends. A store that Next enters for part of a request, like a cached function's store, or leaves for part of it, like a Server Action's store for the render after the action, is put back after an `await` by the code that awaits there, which is compiled to do so: the app's own source files, and three modules of Next's server, in the layer they are of: the wrapper of a `"use cache"` function in the `rsc` layer, and Next's handler of a Server Action and its render in the `ssr` layer. That code also has the stores it was called with back after it awaited a request that the server made to itself, which is the one at work until it ends. A store it had not entered by then still comes from the request at work, and so does what is not compiled. See [The Scope Of A Cached Function](#the-scope-of-a-cached-function).
- **`Buffer`**, **`process`**, and the Node modules that Next's server imports.

The server's console is the page's, so what the server logs is in the output of the test once. In development, React's Flight server sends what a request logs to the page, which logs it again. The plugin turns that off. React would also send what client code logs while a request is open, as that code reads the request's scope (see `AsyncLocalStorage` above), and its response could stay open.

For the browser side, the plugin stands in for a page load (`page.ts`). The browser cannot navigate away: that would unload the test. So once the whole server document has arrived, the plugin moves it into the test's document, runs its inline scripts in order, and sets the URL with the History API. Of the test's document, its scripts stay, and its `<style>`s, which style what the host shows over the page; the rest steps aside while the page is open, the CSS of the host's modules too: the `<link>` of a chunk in a static build, the stylesheets that `linkStylesheetsOf()` linked for files of the host, and Vite's `<style>` of a module with a dev server, which stays where Vite's client keeps it, switched off with a media that matches nothing. A page has the CSS of its route, as with `next start`, and a node, which renders in the test's document, has the test's as well. Leaving the page puts back the URL that the document had as the page opened, and what stepped aside. The test runs in a page of the plugin's (`browser.testerHtmlPath`), not Vitest's own, which has a reset, `body { margin: 0 }`, and Vitest puts that reset in its own page only. So a page, and a node, has the margin of the browser and the CSS of the app, as with `next start`. A project's own `testerHtmlPath` wins. React's scripts in the document wait for a frame before they put streamed content in place, so the plugin has them do it right away. The document has therefore loaded when Next's client starts, and a page's first load does not show a `loading.tsx` or a Suspense fallback. A navigation in the app does, see [Open A Whole Route](../nextjs-guide.md#open-a-whole-route).

A navigation that the app makes without its router, a `<form>`, a plain `<a href>` or `location.assign()`, the plugin makes as a browser does (`navigate()` in `page.ts`): the page that is open stays until the answer is there, the request goes through the app as a page load's does, and then the answer is the next page. A later navigation stops it, and so does the test when it moves on. A navigation whose answer is a download is downloaded instead, and the page stays as it is: the navigation of an `<a download>`, or an answer with `Content-Disposition: attachment`, like a route handler's `.xlsx`. The plugin hands the body to the browser as a file (`downloads.ts`): a Blob URL that an `<a download>` clicks, which the browser saves, and the URL goes right after. The name is the `filename*` or `filename` of `Content-Disposition`, which a browser takes over the link's, else the `download` attribute, else the last segment of the URL. An `<a download>` loads no page, so it stops no other navigation, and a later one does not stop it; its URL can be a file of `public/`, which the network has. An answer that is not ok is no file, and an uncaught error. A download needs no page of the app, so it goes the same way from a link of the test in a browser context of the app without a page. Outside a context, as in a test file with `"use client"`, the app has no navigation: see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client). A test sees it as the click of an `<a download>` whose `href` is a Blob URL: spy on `HTMLAnchorElement.prototype.click`, and fetch the URL in the spy, before the plugin revokes it. Any other answer that is not HTML, like JSON, is an uncaught error: a browser would show it in place of the app, which a test cannot, and the page stays.

For a `redirect()` in a response that had started, Next sends a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` for a browser without JavaScript, and its router loads the page it redirects to when it finds that tag. A browser drops a refresh that is still pending with the page. This document stays, so the plugin takes the `http-equiv` off the tag before it moves it in: the router still finds the tag, and nothing comes due a second later, in the page that is there by then.

The entry of the history that a document was loaded in is `navigation.activation` of the Navigation API. Here that is the test's entry, from before the tests navigated. Next's router takes a current entry other than that one, with its own state on it, for a back or forward navigation that it missed while it hydrated, and restores itself from that state: the page renders again as it loads, with a new object of `useParams()`. So while a page is open, its `activation` is the entry it was loaded in, and leaving the page puts back the document's.

A build knows two things that a request has to find out here:

- **Server Actions.** Next's build lists every action in the app. Here an action is the module and the export that its id names (`<module>#<export>`). So for a `POST` with a `next-action` header, the server checks whether that id names a Server Action, and lists only that one. An id that names none gets the response Next gives when it has no such action: `409`, with `x-nextjs-action-not-found`. Next answers an id that cannot be one with `400`. Here an id can be one when it is shaped like Next's own, 42 characters, or like Vite RSC's. When the action's module fails to load, that error is the response, a `500`.
- **Vite's client.** Vite imports `/@vite/client` into a module with CSS, with `import.meta.hot`, or with a dynamic import it cannot analyse, like the one that loads a Client Component by its id. The `ssr` and `browser` layers load through a module runner, and they get the client the page already has. `vitestPluginRSC()` arranges that for every environment that the page runs through a module runner (`src/vite-client.ts`). A copy of their own would open a websocket per page load, and not to the page's server. A module in a runner has a file URL, so Vite's client falls back to the port the dev server was configured with. That is another server when the port was taken, as it is while a second Vitest run is active on the machine. That server refuses the copy, which then logs an error that it cannot connect. Or the copy reloads the tab: MSW's replacement of `WebSocket` reports `open` before there is a connection, so Vite's client takes the refusal for a server that went away, and reloads once that other server answers its ping.

Next loads `next.config.ts` itself. It compiles the file and runs the result as a module without a filename, so Node resolves the config's relative imports, like `./env.ts`, from the working directory. For `next build` that is the project. For Vitest it can be the workspace root. So the plugin makes the project the process's working directory while Next loads the config, one project at a time.

## Caching

Next's Data Cache works. What `unstable_cache` computes is kept for the next request. So is what a `fetch` gets with `cache: "force-cache"` or `next: { revalidate }`, with or without `next: { tags }`. Two `fetch` calls for the same URL in one render are one request.

Invalidation works as it does in a deployment: `revalidateTag()` and `revalidatePath()` from a Server Action or a route handler, and `updateTag()` and `refresh()` from a Server Action, which is the only place Next allows those two.

Next's server makes an `IncrementalCache` for a request. Here the plugin makes it, and gives it to Next for every request. The class is Next's. So is the handler it picks, the one `next start` uses, and so is where it keeps the entries: on the disk, in the directory of the build, as `next start` keeps them in `.next/`. The disk is [the server's](#the-servers-disk), which `cleanup()` empties, and the directory is `/.next/<n>` for the `n`th test, so a request of an earlier test that is still running writes into its own. Not in Next's memory store, which is one for the process. The options are the ones Next's server passes. Pages and route handlers share one cache.

From `next.config`, `experimental.fetchCacheKeyPrefix` applies, and `cacheMaxMemorySize` to the handlers of `"use cache"` below. So do `cacheHandler`, the class of the handler of this cache, and `cacheHandlers`, the handler of each kind of `"use cache"`: the plugin loads them before the first request, as Next's server does, in the `ssr` layer. A handler of CommonJS is compiled as a source file of the app is: see **CommonJS** in [The Compiler](#the-compiler). Next's route module makes a cache of its own for its response cache, which imports the handlers by their file: here it gets the one above.

Every test starts with an empty cache. `cleanup()` empties the disk the entries are on, forgets the revalidated tags and gives the cache a new key prefix, so no test finds what an earlier one stored. That also holds for a cached function that was still running when its test ended and stores its result afterwards. A cached function that only starts after its test has ended stores its result for the next test.

There is a cache between requests too, so a test can call a function of `unstable_cache` itself and share what it computes with the page. Await it before the next request, because a cached function that is still running when a request starts hands that request its cache scope.

Next compares an entry with a revalidation by their timestamps in milliseconds, from `Date.now()`. `vi.useFakeTimers()` stops the clock, and so does `vi.setSystemTime()` on its own. With a stopped clock, a tag that is revalidated in a later request than the one that stored the entry is not newer than the entry, so the entry stays. An entry's age, which `revalidate` uses, is off by the difference from the real clock.

### Prerendered Pages

With `build: "production"` the server keeps what `next build` prerenders, as `next start` serves it. Next's build decides that for each route, at build time, and writes it to `.next/prerender-manifest.json`; Next's server only reads that file. Here the plugin asks Next for the verdict at a route's first request, and lists it in the manifest, which `build-output.ts` answers for, at its first page load or navigation. A prefetch never prerenders a route: Next's router prefetches every link in view, and a prerender renders the whole page, also one that turns out to read the request. So a prefetch, a request with `next-router-prefetch: 1` and `rsc: 1` as Next's handler tells one, renders the route as a dynamic route, from a manifest without it, also once it is kept; a path that a route with `dynamicParams = false` leaves out gets the not-found page, as from `next start`. A full prefetch, of `<Link prefetch={true}>`, sends no `next-router-prefetch` header: it prerenders the route as a navigation does. The verdict has two parts:

- The verdict on the paths of the route, from what Next's build calls in its worker for each route, on the route module: `collectSegments()`, `collectRootParamKeys()` and `buildAppStaticPaths()`, which runs `generateStaticParams`. Then the lines of `build/index.js` that make the paths of that, which Next has in no function of its own: `prerender-verdict.ts` has them, with their line numbers. A page without params is listed at its own pathname. A page with params is prerendered at the paths `generateStaticParams` lists; another path is prerendered at its first request, or with `dynamicParams = false` answered with the not-found page, as `next start` answers it. Without `generateStaticParams`, a page with params is dynamic, unless it has `dynamic = "error"` or `"force-static"`. A route handler is listed where Next's export of one would prerender it: `dynamic = "force-static"` or `"error"`, a `revalidate` of more than 0 or `false`, `generateStaticParams`, a metadata route, or any `GET` with Cache Components. A route handler without a `GET` is not: the build prerenders a route handler with a `GET`, which it answers with 405, so `next start` runs its `POST` at every request. A route of the edge runtime is not, and the route of a node is none of the build's: its route module reads a prerender manifest of its own, which lists nothing.
- The verdict of the render, which is Next's handler's: it prerenders a route the manifest lists at its first request, and keeps the result in the server's cache, as it does for one that was revalidated. A page that reads the request, with `cookies()`, `headers()` or `searchParams`, bails out of the prerender, where Next's build would have found it dynamic. Next's handler answers that with its error page, a 500 that it reports to the server; or, for a page that reads the request in a `<Suspense>` boundary, or has `revalidate = 0`, it throws "Page changed from static to dynamic at runtime" after the render. A `force-dynamic` page bails out before it renders a component. In each case the server takes the route out of the manifest and asks the handler once more, which renders it as a dynamic page. That is not logged: the server hands Next's route modules the logger of the errors of a request, as `next start` does, and it leaves the bail-outs out. So the first request of such a page in production renders it twice, where `next start` renders it once: a mock with a value for one call, like `mockResolvedValueOnce()`, spends it on the prerender. `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` avoids that. A route with `generateStaticParams` that one path of makes dynamic is dynamic for all its paths from then on, where the build keeps the others, and so is a route handler whose prerender failed with an error; both for the rest of the test file, as the verdict of one build.

The verdicts are the code's, and stay from one test to the next. The kept pages are not: they are on the server's disk, as `next start` keeps them in `.next/`, which `cleanup()` empties (see [The Server's Disk](#the-servers-disk)). What an app's own `cacheHandler` keeps of them is expired as `revalidatePath("/", "layout")` expires it, by the implicit tag of the root layout that every page and route handler Next prerenders has; not under a stopped clock, see [Caching](#caching). A page of a parallel route's slot is kept with 200, as the build keeps it, also where another slot has no page for its path: a page load of it shows the not-found page there, and a navigation to it keeps the page that is there. A kept page answers with `x-nextjs-cache: HIT`, the first with `MISS`, with the `Cache-Control` Next gives it, and `revalidate` and `revalidatePath()` work as in a deployment. A request of a kept route with another method than `GET` or `HEAD` gets `405`, as Next's server answers it, unless it may be a Server Action. The fetches of `generateStaticParams` are in the same cache as the page's, as a build's are `next start`'s.

`build: "development"` lists nothing, as `next dev` prerenders nothing: every request renders its page.

What differs from a build: the prerender runs at the first request, not before the tests, and not with `NEXT_PHASE` set to `phase-production-build`, so a page that skips its data at build time shows the test's data. What a build logs as it prerenders is logged at that request. A page that `next build` stops at, like one that reads `useSearchParams()` outside a `<Suspense>` boundary, answers 500 here, with Next's message in the output. With Cache Components the pages are not prerendered: their prerender is in stages that the plugin does not run, see [The Node.js Runtime](#the-nodejs-runtime). Their route handlers are, and Next tells uncached IO in one apart by two turns of `setImmediate`, which is `setTimeout` here: a mock that answers within one can be kept where a build finds the handler dynamic.

### `"use cache"`

A function with the `"use cache"` directive is cached, in an app with `cacheComponents` in its `next.config`. What it returns is kept for the next request with the same arguments, until one of its tags is revalidated. The directive is taken on a function, on a component, on a function that closes over a value, which is a part of its key like an argument, and at the top of a module, for every function the module exports. Two calls with the same arguments in one render are one call: Next's compiler puts React's `cache()` around the function, and so does the plugin, once for every function, also for one that closes over a value and is made anew with each call of the function around it. In the function, `cacheTag()` tags the entry, also after an `await`, `cacheLife()` is taken, and a cached function of its own works, whose tags count for the outer one too. `cookies()` throws in it, as in a deployment.

Next's build compiles such a function with the part of its SWC transform that also compiles Server Actions, which is Vite RSC's here. So the plugin compiles the directive, with the transforms of Vite RSC, into what Next's compiler makes of it: a call of Next's own wrapper, `cache()` of `next/dist/server/use-cache/use-cache-wrapper`. The key of an entry, the cache handler, the tags and the lifetimes are that wrapper's work, which is Next's runtime. As Next's compiler does, the plugin hands it the arguments that the function declares. What a caller passes on top of those, like the index that `map()` passes, is no part of the key. And like Next's compiler, it runs on the source files of the app: a function with the directive in a test file is not cached.

The handler is the one of `cacheHandlers` for the kind of the directive, or else Next's default one, which keeps the entries in memory. It is not the `IncrementalCache` above, and it has no key prefix. Next keys an entry by the id of the function, its arguments, and the `deploymentId` of `next.config` or else the id of the build. The id is a hash of the file and the name of the function, in hex as Next's is. The plugin adds a number to it, which changes when `cleanup()` resets the caches, so a test starts without the entries of an earlier one here too. A handler of the app's sees that id in the key, and keeps what it stored between the tests.

Next stamps the revalidation of a tag with its time rounded to a millisecond, which can be half a millisecond ahead. A request in that half millisecond gets the old entry once, while Next computes the new one. That goes for a deployment too, but a test can send its next request that soon: wait a millisecond after a revalidation.

What is not as in a deployment:

- **Cached Navigations is off.** Cache Components turns `experimental.cachedNavigations` on. With it Next renders a page in stages, so that the browser can keep the static part of a page it navigated to, and the stages lean on the order of `setImmediate` in Node's event loop: see [The Node.js Runtime](#the-nodejs-runtime). The plugin sets it to `false`, also when `next.config` sets it. What the server caches is the same.
- **No page is prerendered.** With Cache Components a prerender is in stages that the plugin does not run (see [Prerendered Pages](#prerendered-pages)), so every request renders its page. `next build` stops at a page that reads the request outside a `<Suspense>` boundary: "Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data during prerendering". Here such a page renders. Route handlers are prerendered.
- **A cached function is no Server Action.** Next's compiler makes a function with the directive a Server Action too, so that a Client Component can get it as a prop, or import it from a module with the directive at its top, and call it. Here React refuses to pass it to the client, and a Client Component that imports it runs its module in the browser.
- **A test cannot call the function itself.** Next's wrapper throws without the stores of a request: call the function through a page or a route handler.
- **A module with the directive at its top** has what it exports cached. A function in it that has the directive itself and is not exported is not cached. Next's compiler caches it.
- **The scope of the function** is that of its own code: see [below](#the-scope-of-a-cached-function).

Next's own tests of `"use cache"`, Cache Components and the handlers of a cache run here: see `docs/next-conformance.md`. What they do not cover is not tested: how long an entry lives with `cacheLife()`, and a `page.tsx` or a `layout.tsx` with the directive.

### The Scope Of A Cached Function

While a cached function runs, Next keeps a store for it in `AsyncLocalStorage`. That store is how `cookies()` knows to throw inside a cached function, how `cacheTag()` finds the entry to tag, and how a `fetch` in it knows not to be cached on its own.

Node carries that store to the code after an `await` in the cached function, and to nothing else. A browser carries nothing: when code runs after an `await`, nothing says whether it belongs to the cached function or to a component next to it that is rendering in the meantime. So an async function is compiled to say so itself. This is what [unctx](https://github.com/unjs/unctx) does for Nuxt:

```js
async function getQuote(topic) {
  const call = h.e();
  try {
    const quote = h.r(call, await h.s(call, load(topic))); // await load(topic)
    cacheTag("quotes");
    return quote;
  } finally {
    h.x(call);
  }
}
```

`e` remembers the stores the function was called with. `s` leaves them right before the function waits, and `r` puts them back when it goes on. A `catch` and a `finally` put them back too, for an `await` that rejects, and `x` leaves them when the function is done. So the stores of a cached function are the current ones only while its own code runs. React renders the rest of the page in the meantime, and reads the store of the request. Nothing of the browser is patched: not `Promise`, not a timer.

Two kinds of module are compiled this way, in every app:

- The source files of the app that are [server code](#server-code-in-the-browser) in the `rsc` layer, which is where the app enters a store. So not a test file.
- The modules of Next's server that await inside a store, one they entered or left with `exit()`, or their request's own, each in the layer it is a module of and for the store it carries. In the `rsc` layer, the wrapper of a `"use cache"` function, `next/dist/server/use-cache/use-cache-wrapper.js`, which enters the scope and awaits before it has React call the function. In the `ssr` layer, through `app-page/module`, the handler of a Server Action, `app-render/action-handler.js`, which enters the action's store, awaits the action, and leaves the store with `exit()` for the render after it, which it awaits; and the render, `app-render/app-render.js`, which awaits the handler and its own work before it starts React's. The list is `nextModulesWithStores` in `compat/paths.ts`. The dependency optimizer of each layer compiles that layer's, and so does a static build.

`e` takes the stores the function is called with as they are then, those of the request included, as Node's context does: not what the request has when the function goes on, which an `exit()` may have changed by then. So does `AsyncLocalStorage.bind()`. A function or a bound callback of a render that outlives its test puts nothing back in the next one.

And one callback has the stores of the code that passed it, as on Node.js: the one that React's Flight server in the `rsc` layer queues a microtask with. That module is compiled to call the server's own `queueMicrotask`, as server code calls the server's `fetch`. React starts a render in a microtask, and that is how Next has React call a cached function: in the scope it entered for the function, and in React's own store for that render. No other module calls it.

React renders in steps, and starts the later ones when a promise it waits for settles, like that of an async component. On Node.js such a step has the stores of the step that waited. Here it has none, so the `performWork()` of the Flight server, which does one step, is compiled to run each step of a render with the stores of its first. So what a cached component returns renders in its scope, as in a deployment: `cookies()` throws in a component under it, `cacheTag()` tags its entry, and a cached component under it adds its tags to it. The run stops with an error when the Flight server has no `performWork()` to compile.

So the code of a cached function has its scope, before and after an `await`, and so has a function of the app that it calls, and what it renders. That goes for `"use cache"`, and for `unstable_cache`. What is not compiled reads the store of the request, where `cookies()` works and `cacheTag()` throws:

- **A callback**, of `then()`, of a timer, or of `process.nextTick()`, which is the browser's `queueMicrotask` here. Only `await` is compiled.
- **What a thenable does in its `then()`**, like a query builder that runs its query when it is awaited. `await` calls `then()` a microtask later, after the function has left its scope to wait. The value comes back to the function, in its scope.
- **A package.** The code in `node_modules` is not compiled, other than the modules of Next's server above, so a function of a package has no scope after an `await` of its own. Your function has it back when the package returns.
- **A function with a `for await` or an `await using`, and an async generator.** They wait where the compile step has no call to put, so they are left as they are, and have no scope after their first `await`.

The same goes for a store that is left for a part of a request, with `exit()`. Next leaves the store of a Server Action for the render after the action, and awaits that render: the render starts in the frame of the `exit()`, outside the store, so what it renders has no action store, and a `redirect()` in a component replaces the page, as in a deployment. Next's handler is compiled, and has the action's store back after that `await`, as on Node.js. So has what the action started before the `exit()` and compiled or bound code goes on with: a promise the action passed to `after()` that calls `headers()` once the action is done, or the action's own code after an `await`. What is not compiled reads the exited store for the rest of the request. That also goes for two places where Next leaves `workUnitAsyncStorage` with an `exit()` whose callback returns a promise: the render of an `ImageResponse` that Cache Components keeps, in `og/cache-image-response.js`, and a span of OpenTelemetry started with `startActiveSpan()`, in `instrumentation-node-extensions.js`.

And the same goes for the stores of the request itself, while the server makes a request to itself, like a Server Action that calls a route handler of the app. The inner request is the one at work until it ends, also after its response, while its `after()` callbacks run, and code that is not compiled reads its stores. Next's handler and render are compiled, so the page after such an action renders with the stores the handler was called with: its own request's cookies, not the empty ones of a route with `dynamic = "force-static"`. A store the outer request had not entered when the handler was called, like the one of an `after()` task, still comes from the inner request while it is at work, as on Node.js it would not.

In a worker of Node.js none of this is compiled: the server's `AsyncLocalStorage` is Node's own, which carries every store as on `next start`, also to a callback, a thenable, a package and a `for await`. `createServerCode()` is told so as the config is resolved (`AsyncContext` in `server-code.ts`), and leaves the app's source files, Next's modules in `nextModulesWithStores` and React's Flight server as they are; the pre-bundles have it in their key. The plugin's own store of the page a request opens, `openedByRequest`, stays the browser's, entered for the request as above: with nothing compiled it is the request's while the request runs alone, and after an `await` it is the one entered last, so of two requests at once the first can read the second's, like its `ssr` or whether it renders a redirect. The speed feature `immediates` runs its task with Node's `setImmediate()`, which keeps the stores, where a message of a `MessageChannel`, as a browser's host sends it, would drop them (`PageHost.serverImmediate()`). The tests of `playground/nextjs-cache-components-demo` run there too, in both modes, where the callback of a timer in a cached function tags its entry.

## Server Code In The Browser

A browser has a `window`, and a `fetch` that Next has not patched. A browser cannot lose its globals, but a module can be compiled so that it does not see them. That is what happens to the modules of a server layer: your JavaScript and TypeScript source files, and the dependencies Vite pre-bundles.

- `typeof window` is replaced by `"undefined"`. `next build` does the same to the code it compiles for a server, and libraries rely on it to tell a server from a browser. The same goes for `typeof document`, `typeof location`, `typeof localStorage` and `typeof sessionStorage`, which are `"undefined"` on a server without help.
- `fetch`, `Request` and `Response` are the server's, even when they are written as `globalThis.fetch`. So a `fetch` in your server code is the one Next patches: two calls for the same URL in one render are one request. The browser still makes the request, so its rules for a request apply, like CORS.
- `AbortController` and `AbortSignal` are the server's too, of the same web APIs as its streams, which Next pipes a response with a signal of its own: in a browser they are the page's, and in a worker of Node.js the runtime's, not the DOM's, which Bun's native `pipeTo()` takes no signal of.

Apart from `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`, which become the server's, nothing else is replaced. Code that reads `window.innerWidth` without checking `typeof window` first throws on a server, and reads the browser's `window` here.

The async functions in the source files of the `rsc` layer are compiled as well, to keep the stores of `AsyncLocalStorage` across an `await`: see [The Scope Of A Cached Function](#the-scope-of-a-cached-function). Not in a worker of Node.js, whose own `AsyncLocalStorage` keeps them.

A Client Component is a module in two layers. It is told it has no `window` while Next renders it to HTML in `ssr`, and it has one in `browser`.

The `rsc` layer shares its Vite environment with the test, and a test needs the browser. So in that environment these are not server code:

- the test files and setup files from your Vitest config: `test.include` and `test.setupFiles`,
- Vitest, Vite and the `@vitest/*` packages you have installed, and the packages those depend on, but for one that your app lists in `dependencies` (the same copy), which is your app's,
- what you list in `browserModules`.

Everything else in that environment is server code, including a module that only a test imports and a file with in-source tests.
