A component defined in a test file is part of that test file's code, and sees the browser. A test file with `"use client"` is code of the `browser` layer, and so is what it imports.

Server code reads `process.env` as on a server. Here it has the project's test env: see [Environment Variables](#environment-variables).

### `browserModules`

Code checks `typeof window` for one of two reasons, and they need opposite answers here.

- **Role.** The code wants to know whether it is the server side of this app. `@t3-oss/env-core` asks, and only hands out a server variable if the answer is yes. `next-themes` asks, and reads no theme from storage on the server. The answer has to be: you are the server.
- **Capability.** The code wants to know whether there is a DOM it can work on. Testing Library asks before it binds `screen` to `document.body`. The answer has to be the truth: you are in a browser. The exception is a module that also gets by without a DOM: told it is on a server, it works all the same.

Nothing in the code says which of the two a module means. So every other module in the `rsc` environment gets the first answer, and `browserModules` lists the ones that need the second:

```ts
vitestPluginNext({
  // Glob patterns, relative to the project root. One for a package starts
  // with `**`: files are matched by their real path, which package managers
  // put elsewhere than in `node_modules/<name>` under the root.
  browserModules: ["test/**", "**/node_modules/@testing-library/**"],
});
```

When you need it, as far as this has been tried:

- A source file that is not a test file or a setup file and that checks `typeof window` or `typeof document` before it works on the page. Without an entry it is told it is on a server. The demo has one in `test/`.
- A package that the tests use on the page and that makes the same check first. `@testing-library/dom` is one: without an entry `screen.getByRole()` throws "For queries bound to document.body a global document has to be available".

When you do not:

- A helper or a package that touches `document` without checking first. Only `typeof` is replaced.
- The locators, `userEvent` and `expect.element` from `vitest/browser`, and the rest of Vitest.
- MSW. Vitest leaves it out of pre-bundling, so it is served as it is.
- PGlite, in memory and on IndexedDB. It looks for a browser by `globalThis.window`, which is not replaced, and finds one.

A package that both the tests and the app use can only get one of the two answers. If it needs both, it cannot be used on both sides. And an entry does not help one of the app's packages that, when told it is on a server, takes a code path only Node.js has.

What this does not cover:

- Everything else a browser has: `navigator`, `self`, `history`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `HTMLElement`, `indexedDB`, `matchMedia`, `requestAnimationFrame`. A library that looks for one of those to tell a browser from a server still finds it.
- Code that looks up a global at runtime: `globalThis.window`, `self.window`, `"window" in globalThis`.
- Code that reads `window` without checking `typeof window` first. On a server that throws a `ReferenceError`. Here it reads the browser's `window`.
- Files that are not JavaScript or TypeScript when Vite loads them, like `.vue` or `.mdx`, and modules that another plugin generates.
- Dependencies in files other than `.js`, `.mjs` and `.cjs`, and a dependency that `optimizeDeps.exclude` leaves out of pre-bundling. Those are served as they are. Vitest leaves out `msw`.
- With `resolve.preserveSymlinks`, Vitest's packages are not recognized.

## Environment Variables

A page sees the project's test env, and a site never a `.local` file. The page's `process.env` has the variables of Next's env files for its test mode: a run reads `.env.test.local`, `.env.test` and `.env`, a build reads `.env.test` and `.env`. A name has the value of the first file that has it, as with Next. The same server code runs in a test, where Next's test mode reads these files, and in a run of another host: the page has one env in both. A build is a site that others download, so it reads no `.local` file, also not `.env.test.local`: a `.local` file holds the secrets of one machine.

What the page's `process.env` has:

- The variables of those files, parsed and expanded by the project's own `@next/env`, as Next does it. A `$VAR` is expanded against the files alone: a name that only the shell has is empty here, where `next` would read it from the shell.
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables of those files, in every layer: not as constants in the code, as Next inlines them, but in `process.env`, which a module reads as it runs. Next's constants for the dependencies leave them out, so a new value does not make Vite pre-bundle the dependencies again. A dependency that reads one as it evaluates is not trimmed to one branch either.
- `env` of `next.config`. The config is evaluated in the host's process, so a name that the env files have too has the value of the files. A name that only `env` has keeps the value the config gave it, which can come from the shell or `.env.local`, as `next build` inlines it too: the app made it public itself. A build lists those names apart.

And what it does not have, apart from what `env` of `next.config` puts in: `.env.local`, `.env.development*` and `.env.production*`, and no value that the host's process has from elsewhere, like the shell, CI, or env files that the host loaded itself. `NODE_ENV`, `NEXT_RUNTIME` and the names that start with `__NEXT_` are Next's own: the app's `NODE_ENV` stays as it is (see [Development Or Production](#development-or-production)).

The plugin fills `process.env` before any module of the app evaluates, in every layer, with a dev server and in a build, for each name that the page does not have yet: a library that validates the env as it loads, like t3-env, has it. A test or a setup file that assigns a name changes it for the code that reads it after that. The layers share the page's one `process.env`, so the `browser` layer has the server's variables too: a Client Component that reads one is a bug of the app, which Next leaves undefined in the browser, and here it passes.

A run says which env files it read, as an info line of Vite's logger, which Vitest shows with `logLevel: "info"`. A build says the files, and the names that it puts into the site, never their values. Every value of `.env.test` and `.env` is in the files of a build: keep secrets out of them. A secret that the tests need on one machine goes in `.env.test.local`.

Before Next's config is loaded, the host's process gets the variables of the test env that it does not have, so that a `next.config` that validates the env sees them. A host that loaded env files of its own before, like `.env.development` and `.env.local` for a dev server, keeps its value of a name that both have: the config is validated with that value, while the page gets the one of the test env.

With a dev server, a change of an env file loads the page again with the new env. A change of one that Vite reads for its own mode, like `.env`, restarts the server instead. The dependencies are not pre-bundled again. A new env file needs a restart only where Vite does not watch the root of the project.

An app with its values only in `.env.development`, for `next dev`, has none of them here. Move them to `.env`, which every mode reads, to `.env.test`, or for one machine to `.env.test.local`. What a host puts in `import.meta.env`, like the variables of its own prefix, still comes from the env files that the host reads for its mode: `process.env` comes from the test env.

## Mocks

`vi.mock()` replaces a module in the `rsc` layer, where the test runs. That is the module your Server Components and Server Actions import. The other two layers load their own modules, so a mock does not reach a Client Component. A test file with `"use client"` cannot mock either. It runs in the `browser` layer with the page's `vi`, whose mocker replaces what the page imports: the modules of the `rsc` layer, not the ones that the `browser` layer's module runner fetches for the file. So the plugin stops with an error at a `vi.mock()`, `vi.unmock()`, `vi.doMock()`, `vi.doUnmock()` or `vi.hoisted()` in it. Pass a mock to a component as a prop instead.

Mocks of app modules go in a setup file. With `isolate: false` the test files of a worker share their modules, so a module is mocked for all of them or for none, and the file that loads it first decides. A setup file runs before every test file. A bare `vi.mock("./app/lib/weather.ts")` there is enough, and a test says what the mock does with `vi.mocked(getForecast).mockResolvedValue("sunny")`.

This needs Vitest 5.0.4 or later. In browser mode, Vitest 5.0.3 does not wait for a setup file's mocks before it imports a test file, so a test file with no `vi.mock()` of its own gets the real module ([vitest-dev/vitest#11450](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/issues/11450)).

## The Node.js Runtime

Next has two server runtimes. A route picks one with `export const runtime`, and gets `nodejs` without it. The other one, `edge`, is closer to a browser, but Next has deprecated it: `next build` in 16.4 warns about it, and Cache Components, `"use cache"` and `proxy.ts` only exist for Node.js. So the server layers are compiled for Node.js, for every route. A route that asks for `edge` runs on Node.js too. A run says so once when it starts, and lists the files.

`process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME` is a compile-time constant, and with `nodejs` Next's code takes its Node.js server's branches. Three things differ from `next start`, because a browser has web APIs and no Node.js ones:

- Web streams. `process.env.__NEXT_USE_NODE_STREAMS` is Next's own compile-time switch between `renderToPipeableStream` and `renderToReadableStream`. `getDefineEnv()` turns it on for Node.js, and the plugin turns it off.
- React's builds for web streams: `react-dom/server.edge`, and Vite RSC's Flight codec. So the server layers have Next's alias tables for its edge runtime, with one rule for `react-dom/server` and `react-dom/static` of the ssr layer, which differ by runtime: Next's own files get the edge table's, as its renderer runs on web streams, and the app's code, its files and its packages, the Node.js ones. A Client Component that imports `react-dom/server` or `react-dom/static` gets React's entry for Node.js, as a route on Node.js does: `renderToString()` and `renderToStaticMarkup()`, and the stream renderers, on the stand-ins for `stream` and `util` below. Next's `stream-ops.web`, which imports them too, gets React's builds for web streams.
- Next's ESM files, and its route modules as modules. For Node.js Next loads one bundle of its own, `next/dist/compiled/next-server/app-page.runtime`, which includes React for both server layers.

This is what a Node.js server has and a browser does not. The modules of Node.js are the package's, in `src/node/` (see below), Next's own modules of its process in `node-platform.ts`, the request and the response in `node-server.ts`, the files of `.next/` in `build-output.ts`, and the globals in `globals.ts`:

| What                                                     | Here                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `http.IncomingMessage`, `http.ServerResponse`            | The request is a stream of its body, with the properties Next reads from it. The response is Next's own stand-in for one, `MockedResponse` from `server/lib/mock-request`, which Next uses for the requests it makes to itself. It becomes a `Response` at its first byte. A reader that cancels its body closes it, as a browser that leaves does, and so does Next's handler when it is done without a head                           |
| The manifests in `.next/`                                | `load-manifest.external`, the module Next keeps out of its bundle to read them, answers from memory. The routes manifest is the one Next's build makes, with `generateRoutesManifest()`. The prerender manifest lists what Next's verdict on a route prerenders, in production, as the route is first requested: see [Prerendered Pages](#prerendered-pages)                                                                            |
| A route handler's request handler                        | Next's own, `templates/app-route`, as `next start` calls it: `handler(req, res, ctx)`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| A page's request handler                                 | Next's own, `templates/app-page-runtime`, as `next start` calls it: `handler(req, res, ctx)`. It makes the route module in the `rsc` layer, and gets the `ssr` layer's class for it, and its contexts of Next's `*.shared-runtime` modules, where Next's build for Node.js sends an import of one in the server layers. So `next/router` loads in a Server Component, as on `next start`: React's server build has no `createContext()` |
| `node:stream`, `stream/promises`                         | readable-stream 4, the streams of Node.js 18 as a package, with `Readable.from()`, `addAbortSignal()` and `promises`, and the bridge to web streams, `Readable.toWeb()` and `fromWeb()`, added. The package's `vitest-plugin-rsc/node/stream`; unenv's `Readable` reads nothing. `string_decoder` is the string_decoder package                                                                                                         |
| A Server Action's body: busboy, `decodeReplyFromBusboy`  | Next's busboy on that stream. The parts are collected into a `FormData` for Vite RSC's `decodeReply`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `node:crypto`                                            | Web Crypto for random values and `subtle`, with `randomInt()` and `randomFill()` on it. MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2 of @noble/hashes for `createHash` and `hash`, which Next's cache keys need synchronously, and on them `createHmac` and `timingSafeEqual`, which check the signature of a webhook or a JWT. Another algorithm throws, and so do Node's other functions, like `createCipheriv`, `pbkdf2` and `createSign`, which are unenv's |
| `node:zlib`                                              | fflate's deflate, sync and with a callback, for gzip, zlib and raw deflate, which server code commonly compresses with. The framing and the checksums are read here, as zlib reads them; a gzip of more than one member, bytes after a gzip or a zlib, and the options `info`, `flush`, `finishFlush` and a `windowBits` below 15 throw. The streams, Brotli and Zstandard throw, as unenv's                                            |
| `node:path`                                              | path-browserify, the POSIX path of Node.js for a browser, with `posix` and `win32`, which are the same here                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `node:timers`, `timers/promises`                         | The page's timers, and `setImmediate` as above, as promises too, with a `signal`. unenv's resolve at once                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `node:fs`, `fs/promises`                                 | A disk in memory, memfs, which `cleanup()` empties: see [The Server's Disk](#the-servers-disk)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `node:process`                                           | The `process` of the test, as the global is, and unenv's for what it lacks, like `platform`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Node's other modules: `os`, `url`, `buffer`, `http`…     | [unenv](https://github.com/unjs/unenv)'s, made of what a browser has, like `URL` and `performance`. What it has no stand-in for throws when it is called, or answers as a machine without it would: `os.hostname()` is `""`. For a layer that imports the module, and not for a dependency whose `browser` field says what it uses for it: see `node-builtins.ts`                                                                       |
| `setImmediate`                                           | A function in `registry` that server code is compiled to call. It is not a global, because a library in the page that finds a `setImmediate` uses it, as React's scheduler does. With a global one the playgrounds failed now and then on a React `removeChild`                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `process.cwd()`, `nextTick()`, `hrtime`, `on()`, `off()` | Added to the `process` of the test                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| A `Request` with a Node.js stream as its body            | The server's `Request` takes one, as Node's does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `Buffer#latin1Slice()` and the like, which busboy calls  | On `Uint8Array.prototype`, because every copy of the `Buffer` polyfill is a `Uint8Array`. The page shares that global                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| What Next patches when its server starts                 | Left out: `console`, `Date`, `Math.random`, `crypto`, `setImmediate`, the process handlers, the hook on `require`. The globals are the test's too                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `instrumentation.ts`                                     | Not run. Next's own module that loads it, `instrumentation-globals.external`, gets a `require` that finds no file, as Node.js finds none for an app without one                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

These are also there for the app's server code, as far as the stand-ins go. The `browser` layer gets the four modules of Node.js that Next's edge runtime has, from Next's own polyfills, `buffer`, `events`, `assert` and `util`, as before, and nothing for the rest.

In a worker of Node.js ([The Node Host](architecture.md#the-node-host)) the server layers run on Node.js itself, and of the table above only what is about Next's own process stays: the request and the response, the manifests from memory, the request handlers, a Server Action's body, what Next patches as its server starts, `setImmediate`, and `instrumentation.ts`. The rest is Node's own:

- **The modules of Node.js.** Every one is Node's: `node-builtins.ts` gives a server layer `node:<name>` as an external, which the runner imports, in a source file and in a pre-bundle, whose `require()` of one is an import of it (Rolldown's `esmExternalRequirePlugin`). Vite's import analysis names it `/@id/node:<name>` in an environment of a browser, which Vitest's runner of the `rsc` layer takes for the module, and the plugin answers the runner of the `ssr` layer so (`src/index.ts`). A `require()` in the app's CommonJS returns its `module.exports`, its default export. The `browser` field of a package does not apply to them, and `fastCrypto` puts its stand-ins over Node's `node:crypto`. The disk is the machine's: see [The Server's Disk](#the-servers-disk).
- **Resolution.** The server layers resolve with Node's conditions, `node` where a browser has `browser`, and Vite's fields of a package for a server, as Vitest resolves a project of happy-dom or jsdom and Next its server: a package with a build for each, like `jose` or `ws`, is its build for Node.js.
- **`AsyncLocalStorage`.** Node's own, the `node` condition of the package's `./async-hooks`, carries Next's and React's stores across an `await`, a timer and a callback, as on `next start`: nothing is compiled for it, see [The Scope Of A Cached Function](#the-scope-of-a-cached-function).
- **What differs from `next start` still.** One process has the test, the server and the page, which share their globals, `process.env` and the fake timers of a test; a request to the app is a call, not a socket, so a request to the app's own origin through `http`, not `fetch`, reaches the dev server, not the app; the server's `fetch` to the network is Node's own as the worker started, `serverWebApis` of the host, which a `fetch` that a test patches later, like MSW's `setupServer()`, does not see; `process.cwd()` is Vitest's; there is no build output on the disk; a route on the edge runtime runs on Node.js; the server renders with web streams and React's builds for them, as the three differences above say; and Next's staged rendering and `instrumentation.ts` are not there, as in a browser. A native addon, like `sharp` or `bcrypt`, loads where Node.js imports it itself: a package that the app lists in `optimizeDeps.exclude`, which Vitest's runner of the `rsc` layer has Node.js import.

A module of Next that `node-platform.ts` stands in for is replaced by its path, all of it. When a run starts, the plugin checks that each is a file of the installed Next, and stops, with the version of Next, where one is not: its stand-in would be a stand-in for nothing. An export of such a module that its stand-in does not have, one that is new in a Next the plugin was not written for, gets a stub that throws when it is used, naming the export and the version of Next, and the run says so once when it starts. A run that does not use it goes on.

Every module of Node.js that the server layers import is a module of the package, `vitest-plugin-rsc/node/<name>` in `src/node/`, and comes from nowhere else: not Next's polyfills, which only the `browser` layer gets, and not `node-platform.ts`. `scripts/node-modules.ts` writes most of them from unenv's list; `assert`, `buffer`, `crypto`, `path`, `stream`, `stream/consumers`, `stream/promises`, `string_decoder`, `timers`, `timers/promises`, `util` and `zlib` are written by hand, where unenv's is not enough, by the rule of [Which Functions Work](../nodejs-in-the-browser.md#which-functions-work): `assert` is the assert package and `util` the util package with Node's own `inspect()` from node-inspect-extracted, as unenv's compare by JSON and inspect by `JSON.stringify`. The build makes one file of its own of each, with memfs, unenv, readable-stream, fflate or @noble/hashes in it, in `dist/node/`, and that file is what a layer gets, in this repository too: `pnpm test` builds the package first, so that a run of the source behaves as an installed package does. `async_hooks` is the one exception: it is the package's own `vitest-plugin-rsc/async-hooks`, aliased in every layer, which under the `node` condition, that the server layers of a page in a worker of Node.js resolve with, is Node's own. A layer gets the file: Vite serves it as it is, and a build, or the pre-bundle of a dependency that imports the module, like React's renderer for Node.js, bundles it. So it is no dependency for Vite to find and pre-bundle, and a Vite cache older than the import changes nothing: there is nothing to find as a test runs. The page can still evaluate the module more than once, in each layer's module graph, in such a pre-bundle and in the build of each layer, and each evaluation hands out the `AsyncLocalStorage` of the first, the page's global one, which Next's own code takes too: one per page, so that a store a package creates is entered with the request, carried across an `await` and reset between tests, as Next's are. The `browser` layer's too: while a request is open, a store that its code enters lasts for the synchronous part of the callback, as on the server. What such a file imports of Node.js, like memfs `node:events`, is the package's file for it too, not Next's polyfill, which is CommonJS that a layer would have to pre-bundle: the files are all ESM, and a layer pre-bundles nothing for them, the same as without them. Their `stream` is readable-stream 4 and their `events` the events package: unenv's `Readable` reads nothing, and readable-stream calls its `EventEmitter` as a function, which unenv's class is not. The app adds nothing to `optimizeDeps.include`, and `optimizeDeps.noDiscovery` needs no `include` for these. An npm package named like a module of Node.js, such as `url` or `punycode`, is not resolved to the installed package in the server layers but to the module of Node.js, as on Next's server.

What is still to do here:

- Next's staged rendering, which Cache Components uses for a prerender and for Cached Navigations. It needs what a browser does not have at all: the order of `process.nextTick` and `setImmediate` in Node's event loop, and Next's patched `Date` and `Math.random`. The stand-in for `fast-set-immediate.external` throws where that code starts. So Cached Navigations is off: see [`"use cache"`](#use-cache).
- `instrumentation.ts`, which would load where `node-platform.ts` gives Next's module a `require`, and the app's own `cacheHandler`, which would go where `load-manifest.external` and its neighbours are.

## Watch Mode

A test that opens a route with `renderServer({ url })` does not import the files of the route: the plugin's lists of the routes do, and every test file imports those. So in watch mode an edit of a file of the app runs every test file that opens a route, and an edit of a file that a test file imports itself runs that test file too.

`vitest --changed` and `vitest related` pick their test files from Vitest's own import graph, which has the same shape: they find a test file by what it imports, not by the routes it opens. To be sure a change of a route is tested, run the test files that open routes, or the whole suite.

## A Static Build

`vite build` builds the app into a directory of files: see [A Static Build](../static-build.md). It builds Next's production code unless `build: "development"` is set (see [Development Or Production](#development-or-production)), and Vite minifies the three layers, as it minifies the code of any page. The build is one of Vite's app builder, so each environment is built with the others in sight, in this order:

1. The rsc layer, to find the `"use client"` files it refers to. Vite RSC collects them as it compiles.
2. The browser layer, as a scan: it finds the `"use server"` files the Client Components import, which the rsc layer must export, and the packages of the host that its module graph reaches. Nothing is written.
3. The rsc layer again, now with every server reference, and then the browser layer with every client reference, and the ssr layer with the ones that server code reaches.

The rsc layer is the `client` environment, which Vite builds as the page: `index.html` of the host and the chunks of the app's server code. The other two layers run in module runners, as with the dev server (see [Three Layers, Three Environments](#three-layers-three-environments)). A dev server transforms each of their modules on request. A build has no server, so the plugin writes each layer into one file, `vitest-plugin-rsc/<environment>/modules.json`: every chunk of the layer, transformed for the module runner, by its id. A tab fetches the file once and the runner evaluates a module from it as the layer imports it. The browser layer's first: a page of the host whose scripts load the layers has a `<link rel="preload" as="fetch" crossorigin>` for it at the top of its `<head>`, at the URL that Vite names the page's scripts by: from `base`, or for `base: "./"` by the path from the page. The tab's `fetch` of the file takes it, so its request starts before any script of the page has loaded. The file of another layer starts when that layer starts to load: see [Three Layers, Three Environments](#three-layers-three-environments). A host's preload stays in the document while a page of the app is open: it shows nothing, and put back it would fetch its file again. Relative imports between the chunks are the paths of the build, and `import.meta.resolve()` resolves against the URL the chunk would have had as a file.

With a dev server, the id of a module in a Flight payload is the one Vite imports it by. In a build Vite RSC names a reference with a hash of its path, and a file of a package with a hash of the bare specifier it was imported by. A file of Next that the app or a route entry imports is named by that specifier, like `next/dist/client/components/builtin/global-error.js`; one that only Next's own files import, by a relative path, by its specifier in `next/dist/esm`. Neither depends on where `node_modules` has the file, so the name is the same in every build, on any install. That holds while the rsc layer reaches a file one way: an app that imports a Client Component of Next by its path, which Next's files import relatively, gives it two, and it gets the name of whichever Vite RSC saw last. The plugin gives each layer a list of the modules a payload can refer to, by that id: `virtual:vitest-plugin-rsc/client-references` for the ssr and the browser layer, and `virtual:vitest-plugin-rsc/server-references` for the rsc layer. A dev server has neither: the lists are `undefined` there, and the layers import by id. The browser layer's list has every client reference. The ssr layer's has the ones that server code reaches in the module graph of the rsc layer's second build, which gives them their ids: through static and dynamic imports from the plugin's module of the rsc layer, which renders the routes, and from every file of the host that is not a client reference itself, which can render a node, up to a client reference. A file of the host with `"use client"` that a file of `host.files` without the directive imports is in both lists, as is a Client Component of the app that a route renders, also where the file of the host only passes it to `loadClientModule()`. One that only the host's runtime imports, a module that is no file of `host.files`, like an inline module script of a page or a package of the host, is in the browser layer's alone: no server code renders it, so its code, and what only it imports, stay out of the ssr layer's file. So a node's Client Components have to be imported by the app or by a file of `host.files`: one that only the host's runtime imports and passes to `renderServer()` renders with a dev server, and not from a build, where the ssr layer has no module for it ("the build has no Client Component"). Inside a `<Suspense>` boundary React then renders that boundary in the browser instead, with an error in the console. The build of the layers is the one of `vitestPluginRSC()`, which builds its two layers the same way without Next.js (see [A Static Build](architecture.md#a-static-build)): `vitestPluginNext()` gives it the ssr layer, the files of Next's loaders and the stylesheets.

The build can be served from any path, so a file of it names another by the way from itself. Where the plugin's own code, the output of Next's image and font loaders, and a stylesheet need the directory of the build, they have a placeholder: `__VITEST_PLUGIN_RSC_BUILD_DIR__` in JavaScript and `//vitest-plugin-rsc-build-dir` in CSS. Once a chunk has its place in the build, the placeholder becomes the relative path from that chunk to the directory of the build, resolved against the chunk's `import.meta.url`. The files of the host's own build, like the scripts of `index.html`, are named by Vite, from `base`.

The stylesheets of a route are the plugin's to collect, as with the dev server (see [Stylesheets](#stylesheets)): a build knows them from the module graph of each page, as the rsc layer is built, and emits a file per stylesheet under `/_next/static/css/`, named with a hash of its content. The list of each route's stylesheets is in `vitest-plugin-rsc/next-files.json`, with the modules of each route, and the rsc layer reads it in the browser when Next asks for the stylesheets of a route. The page fetches it as it starts, with the layers. Fonts of `next/font` and images that Next's loaders emit are files of the build too, under `/_next/static/media/`.

The file has five keys. `assetPath` is Next's, `/_next/`, which a stylesheet is linked from. `routes` has, for each page route by the name of its modules, the stylesheets of each segment by its key in the loader tree, `app/layout`, as files of the build: `_next/static/css/global-1a2b3c4d.css`. The route of a node has an empty list at `vitest-plugin-rsc/component`. `hostFiles` has, for each file of the host that the rsc layer built, by its path from the root of the project, `host/node.tsx`, the stylesheets it reaches as the dev server walks it: through the files of the app it imports, into the `browser` layer from a Client Component, up to the lists of the routes, in the order of the imports. A file of the host is what `host.files` matches, as a build has no Vitest config. When Next asks for the stylesheets of the route of a node, the page adds those of the files of the host that render the node, in their order and each once, at `vitest-plugin-rsc/component`. A path from the root is normalised, `./host/node.tsx`, and an absolute one, which a build cannot resolve without the machine's paths, is the longest key it ends with. A file that the build has none for warns once in the page, and the node renders without them. `linkStylesheetsOf()` links the stylesheets of a file of `hostFiles` by the same paths, with the directive or without, as with a dev server. `modules` has, for each page route by the name of its modules, the chunks of the rsc layer that it loads, by their index in `chunks`, the files of the build, which many routes share: the chunk of its entry, those of the layouts, pages and boundaries of its loader tree, and every chunk those import, read off the chunks of the build. Not a chunk that a segment imports with `import()`, like a component of `next/dynamic`, which loads when the segment asks for it, and none that the module listing the routes imports, which the page has before any route. Every path is from the root or from the build, and the keys of `hostFiles` are sorted, so the file is the same on every machine.

A page load starts the files of its route at once, as the server renders it, where Next would load the module of each segment only once it has the one around it, and the browser would ask for the stylesheets only once the HTML is there. Before the route's entry loads, the page adds a `<link rel="modulepreload">` for each of its modules, and a `<link rel="preload" as="style">` for each of its stylesheets, at the URL Next links it at, in the CORS mode of `crossOrigin` of `next.config`: the module and the stylesheet take the preload, one request each. Next evaluates the modules when it asks for them, in its own order. Next's development code links a stylesheet with the time of the request in its URL, `?v=`, and a deployment id adds `?dpl=`, which no preload can know: a build of the development code and an app with a `deploymentId` start only the modules. The links are the page's: leaving it takes them. A navigation of the app without its router preloads nothing: the page before it is still open as it is sent, and leaving that page would take the links. A load that the host stops adds none once its request is aborted, and leaving takes what it had added. A load that fails keeps them until the host leaves it or opens the next page, as `cleanup()` does. `handleRequest()`, which loads no page, adds none. A dev server serves a module where the page asks for it.

The plugin puts no path of the machine that builds into a build, so the same tree builds into the same files in any directory, and on any machine: `build-test/` of the e2e demo checks both. These would have one:

- **The loader tree.** Next's app loader imports each layout, page and boundary by its absolute path, and names it by that path in the tree, which Next looks up its stylesheets by. The plugin keeps the import, for Vite to resolve, and names the file by its path from the root of the project, `app/layout.tsx`, with a dev server too (`nameInLoaderTree()` in `src/nextjs/project/entries.ts`). The route entry hands the stylesheet key with each file (`RouteSegment`), so the dev server's lists and `next-files.json` have the key the tree has. The `resolvedPagePath` of a route handler, which Next's errors quote, is that name too. Turbopack names them from a root as well, `[project]/app/layout.tsx`, and Next's runtime reads either.
- **The Next config.** Next's config loader makes `configFile`, `outputFileTracingRoot`, `turbopack.root`, `repoRoot` and `images.loaderFile` absolute, and an app names its cache handlers and adapter by a file. Next's build reads them. Its server reads none for a request but the cache handlers, which the plugin does not load. In a build each of these options is a path from the root of the project (`withPathsFromRoot()` in `src/nextjs/static-build.ts`): `next.config.ts`, `../..`. By the option, and not by what a value looks like: `basePath: "/app"` of a project in `/app` stays. The dev server keeps the config as Next loads it.
- **A compile error.** A module that `next build` stops at throws Next's error when it loads (see [The Compiler](#the-compiler)), and the code frame of SWC's message names the file by its absolute path. It is the path from the root of the project, as `next build` quotes it, with a dev server too.
- **The working directory.** Next's constants have the project's directory from the working directory, `__NEXT_RELATIVE_PROJECT_DIR`, which every route module has. A build from the root of a monorepo would differ from one in the project. It is `""`, as for `next build` in the project, with a dev server too: Next's server joins it to its working directory, which is `/` in the browser.

A file of the host with `"use client"`, like a story file, runs in the `browser` layer of a build as with a dev server, in the graph of the tab (see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client)), from what is there instead of a dev server:

- **Its module.** The `browser` layer has a second entry, `vitest-plugin-rsc/react_client/references.js`: the list of its client references, `virtual:vitest-plugin-rsc/client-references`, by its id in `entries` of the layer. A page's Flight client loads a Client Component from it, and the graph of the tab evaluates a file of the host from it, by the key of the line in front of the file's module, which in a build is a hash. A build has no change, so the file runs once for the document, also for two imports of it, and `loadClientModule()` tells its module by the same export as with a dev server.
- **Its stylesheets.** Those of `hostFiles` in `next-files.json`, which has every file of the host that the rsc layer built. So the line also names the file by its path from the root of the project, not by its id, which is a path of the machine.
- **The packages of the host.** A dev server serves the page the module of a package of `host.packages`, which the runner of the `browser` layer imports from the page. In a build that module is in the host's build, the `rsc` layer, which the host's own scripts are one bundle with: one instance for the host and its files with the directive, like the spies of a testing package of the host. A chunk of the `browser` layer imports it as an external, by the URL a dev server has for it, and the rsc layer has the list of them, `virtual:vitest-plugin-rsc/host-modules`, which imports each one there. The scan of the `browser` layer, step 2 above, finds them for the list in its module graph, not in its chunks: the scan cuts every module down to its imports, so its chunks leave out a module whose package says it has no side effects, and what only that module imports, where the build keeps it for its exports. The layer's own build imports no module of the page that its scan's graph does not reach. The list can have one more than the build imports, which the host's build then bundles, with what it imports, in a chunk that no page loads. A build that imports one the scan's graph did not reach stops with an error that names it.

A layer builds its own entries, not the input of the host: a host with pages of its own, like `index.html` and `callout.html` in `build.rolldownOptions.input`, gets them built as its pages. `playground/nextjs-host-demo` builds so, and its `build-test/` opens both pages from a server of files: a file of the host with `"use client"`, the ones of a package of the host, and `loadClientModule()`, as its tests with the dev server do.

What a build has no equivalent of: the optimizer, so the plugin compiles the dependencies that the optimizer would have compiled with a plugin of the build, and `images.unoptimized` is on in the Next config it loads, unless the app has an image loader of its own.

The site has the env of `.env.test` and `.env`, and of no `.local` file, as one module of each layer, which the page puts in `process.env`: see [Environment Variables](#environment-variables). The build says which names it puts into the site.

## Not Yet

- `ImageResponse` of `next/og`, for an image like `opengraph-image.tsx` that renders one. Next renders the image with WebAssembly and a font of its own, which it reads from its own files with `node:fs`, and the server's disk has no file of the project: the route fails. A page still links the image, with the data the module exports.
- Next's compiler for a package in `node_modules`, apart from a file that names `next/font`. Next also compiles the packages in `transpilePackages`, and a package that uses `next/dynamic`. Here a package is pre-bundled as it is. Not tested.
- A font in a test file. Next's compiler does not run on the test files, so call `next/font` in one of the app's modules. An image that a test file imports is the object Next makes from it.
- Most of a `webpack` function in `next.config`. Its rules with a `test` and the loaders in `use`, like the one of `@next/mdx` for an `.mdx` file, apply: Vite loads such a file with those loaders, and Next's compiler runs after them where the rule names `defaultLoaders.babel`. So do the aliases it sets, the first candidate of a list that resolves. A rule with more than that, like an `issuer`, a change of Next's own rules, and the plugins of webpack it adds do not apply, and a run says so. Also `turbopack` rules, and a Babel config, which makes Next compile with Babel.
- `compiler.emotion`. Next's transform gets the option, but Vite compiles JSX, with its own import source, so the `css` prop needs `jsxImportSource` in your tsconfig. Not tested.
- The React Compiler, `reactCompiler` in `next.config`. Components run as they are written.
- Bundle optimizations: `optimizePackageImports`, `modularizeImports`, `experimental.optimizeServerReact`, the browser targets. They do not change what the app does.
- A `require()` in a source file of the app is an `import`, which runs before the module, also where the call would not run, but for one in a `try` of a module that is not there. A `require()` of what is not a string is left as it is, and throws. See **CommonJS** in [The Compiler](#the-compiler).
- The CSS of a component of `next/dynamic` from Next's manifest of dynamic imports, with `precedence="dynamic"`, next to a preload of its JavaScript. Here it is a stylesheet of the segment that imports the component.
- `experimental.useLightningcss` in `next.config`. Next then compiles CSS with Lightning CSS. Here it is PostCSS, Next's default, so a class of a CSS module has the name of that. A run says so.
- Next's mode of a CSS module, with a PostCSS config that only Vite reads, like `postcss.config.ts`, or with `css.postcss` in the Vitest config. A run says so.
- An asset prefix with its own origin, like a CDN. Stylesheets, font and image files are only served by the dev server, so a page has no CSS.
- The `next.config` headers, and the ones the proxy sets, for a request the app does not answer itself: a file in `public/`, which the dev server serves. Also the `next.config` headers for a request that the proxy answers itself.
- A rewrite, from `next.config` or the proxy, to a path that no route has, like a file in `public/`. The network is asked for the request's URL, not for the rewrite's destination.
- A dynamic route under a folder whose name a URL percent-encodes, like `app/release notes/[id]`. `@next/routing` does not find it. A run warns about it when it starts.
- `i18n` in `next.config`, which belongs to the Pages Router. The app runs as it would without it. An app with `output: "export"` is served like any other, with its proxy and the `next.config` redirects.
- A dynamic segment with a `&` in it, written unencoded. `@next/routing` reads what follows the `&` as a query of the request.
- What `next build` prerenders is prerendered at the first request of its route, not before the tests: what a build logs as it prerenders is not there before, and `NEXT_PHASE` is not `phase-production-build` then. The static shell of a page with Cache Components is not prerendered. See [Prerendered Pages](#prerendered-pages).
- A request the server makes to itself keeps its request stores until all of its work is done, which can be after its response has arrived: an `after()` callback, or a body that streams on. Code that awaits such a `fetch` reads that request's stores until then. For a proxy that is the rest of the request it runs for.
- Next's `instrumentation.ts` is not run, for the proxy or for a route.
- A route handler does not see the query that a rewrite adds, as with `next start`. Its `request.url` is the URL the browser asked for.
- `basePath`, and `trailingSlash: true`. Both are passed to Next's route resolution, and neither is tested with a page.
- A route with `export const runtime = "edge"` runs on Node.js like the others: see [The Node.js Runtime](#the-nodejs-runtime). As `next build` does not prerender a route of the edge runtime, it is not prerendered here, also with `revalidate`: every request runs it. `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME` is a constant in Next's own code and is not set for the app's code.
- Cached Navigations, and the checks of a prerender with Cache Components. A function that is not exported, with the directive, in a module that has it at its top. A function with the directive as a Server Action, which a Client Component gets as a prop or imports. A `page.tsx` with the directive is not tested. See [`"use cache"`](#use-cache).
- The scope of a cached function in a callback, in the `then()` of a thenable, in a package, and in a function with a `for await`: the request's store is read there instead of the cache's. See [The Scope Of A Cached Function](#the-scope-of-a-cached-function).
- Code that is not compiled, like a package's, that exits a store with `AsyncLocalStorage.exit()` for work that awaits, and reads the store again afterwards. The store stays exited for the rest of the request. Next does this for the render after a Server Action, where nothing reads it again.
- An `after()` callback that takes longer than a second continues without its request's stores, so `cookies()` and `headers()` fail in it from then on. For a callback in a source file of the app, which is compiled to keep its stores across an `await`, this is not tested. Under `vi.useFakeTimers()` a response without a body never tells Next it was sent, so its `after()` callbacks do not run while the request lasts, and the next request starts a second late.
- A navigation without Next's router to a route handler that answers with something a browser shows, like JSON, is an uncaught error, because the app would have to make way for it. So is a type that a browser saves because it cannot show it, like a `.zip` without `Content-Disposition: attachment`. A download is downloaded, see [What Stands In For A Server](#what-stands-in-for-a-server). A navigation to another origin, like a redirect to a sign-in or a checkout, is an uncaught error too. The test stays where it is.
- A navigation without Next's router waits for the requests of the page that is open, since the server handles one at a time, and the next page loads once its request is done, `after()` work included: leaving the page before it waits for that work. Without a page, in a browser context of the app, a link to a page of the app is reported once the server has rendered that page, and a form posted to a route handler has run it.
- Server code is only told it is on a server where it checks `typeof window`: see [Server Code In The Browser](#server-code-in-the-browser).
- A mock for Client Components, also in a test file with `"use client"`: see [Mocks](#mocks).
- Next's router and Server Actions in a test file with `"use client"`. Its components render without Next's app, see [A Test File With `"use client"`](#a-test-file-with-use-client). A component that needs them is for `renderServer()`.
- One request at a time. A request that waits for another request that the test has not sent yet will wait forever. A response that streams without end, like server-sent events, holds up every request after it.
- A page that the test leaves before the server has sent anything, because the page waits for data outside a Suspense boundary, is not stopped. Its render continues once the data comes, without its request, and Next logs the errors that follow, possibly in a later test.
- A same-origin `fetch` for a path that a dynamic route matches goes to the app, even when it is for a file in `public/`, which a deployment serves before it looks at the routes. With `app/[locale]/page.tsx` that is every one-segment path, like `/data.json`. With a catch-all at the root, like `app/[...slug]`, it is every path.
- A page that the app loads itself, like after a link without Next's router, gets an entry of the history of its own, as in a browser. `history.back()` to the page before it does not load that page again, as a browser does: Next's router of the page that is open restores it from the state of its entry, with a request for its Flight payload.
- A navigation that leaves the page without Next's router, like `location.assign()`, is turned into a page load with the Navigation API, which today means Chromium.
- Every `renderServer()` loads React and the app's client code again, as a page load does: the modules are evaluated again. They are fetched from the dev server and compiled once, as a browser keeps them in its HTTP cache, until a file changes. Leaving a page also closes its module graph: an `import()` that its code starts after that never settles, and a timer, an interval, an animation frame or an idle callback that its code set does not fire, as a browser drops them with the page, like the timer with which `next-themes` turns transitions back on. For that the `browser` layer compiles each use of `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame` or `requestIdleCallback` as a global, a call, a read, `typeof` or a write, to the timer that the module's runner gives: the global of the moment, also a fake one of the test, which calls nothing once the runner is closed, as a page's is when the page is left (`src/nextjs/page-timers.ts`). One that the code calls on `window` or `globalThis` still fires. A file of the host, like a test file with `"use client"`, keeps the globals, so a spy of its test sees its calls. The plugin releases a page when the test leaves it, by removing what React and Next left on `window` and `document` while they loaded, and every property that was set on the document, `<html>`, `<head>` and the container of a node while the page was open, like the ones in which the page's React DOM keeps the stylesheets it inserted, and the constructed stylesheets that the document adopted while the page was open. A property that a test or a library of the host sets there while a page is open goes with the page too, like a spy that `vi.spyOn(document, "hasFocus")` makes after `renderServer()`, which then stops at the page's end; one from before the page stays. A library that marks the document on its first use is prepared before the first page, see [Another Host Than Vitest](#another-host-than-vitest). What the app's own code leaves there keeps that page in memory, as in a page that never reloads: a listener on `window`, a global. The app has to clean those up, as in an effect's cleanup. A page has its own `<body>`, which goes away with the page, and so does a node. So a portal into `document.body` keeps nothing in memory, though React adds its listeners to the body. The browser itself keeps the element that the pointer is over, and with it its page, until the pointer is over another one. React keeps a page that waited for a stylesheet to load for a minute after, with a timer that it does not clear. In Chromium 153 and later, V8 can keep one page that was left for as long as the tab lives: the first page whose objects extend a shape that the tab shares, like the interop object of a CommonJS package. If the browser grows too much, use `isolate: true`. Every test file then starts in a new page, and loads the app's server again.
- By default React is its development build, including in the server layers, while Next takes itself to be a production server. So the client gets the message of an error that a Server Component throws, and `error.tsx` can show it, where a deployment sends a digest and a message that says nothing. Strict Mode also runs an effect twice. A test that reads the text of such an error passes here and not against a deployment. With `build: "production"` both run as in a deployment: see [Development Or Production](#development-or-production).
- The page has no `cookieStore`. A script that uses the Cookie Store API without checking for it fails. See [Headers And Cookies](#headers-and-cookies).
- A spy on `Storage.prototype` sees no call to the page's `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`, and `Storage.prototype.getItem.call(localStorage, key)` throws. Spy on `localStorage` itself. A `StorageEvent` with the page's storage as its `storageArea` cannot be made: the browser takes only its own, so code that makes one to tell this document of a change throws, like `useStorage()` of VueUse. An `about:blank` iframe that the app makes has the browser's storage. A script that outlives its page, like a persister of a query cache, writes to the browser's own storage once `cleanup()` has closed the context, and to the next test's once that has opened: a write that lands in the browser's storage stays there, for the origin. See [Web Storage](#web-storage).
- A script that outlives its page, like a listener of an event, reads and writes the browser's own cookies once the context is closed, and the cookies of the next test once its context is open: with `document.cookie`, and with a `fetch` of the app.
- MSW writes the `Set-Cookie` of a response it mocks into `document.cookie`, and so into the app's cookies, unless it is `HttpOnly`, which a script cannot write. Also for a `fetch` of the server, whose response a server keeps to itself. And it gives a mocked request the cookies of `document.cookie` for its handler.
- A cookie of the app is a name and a value. Its `Path` and `Domain` do not decide which requests carry it, and one that expires later lasts until the test ends.
- A rewrite to another server does not carry the app's cookies, where `next start` proxies the request with its headers. See [What The Adapter Does Itself](#what-the-adapter-does-itself).
- A `fetch` with Next's `rsc` or `next-action` header is Next's, a request of the router or of a Server Action of the page that is open as it is sent. It never settles once that page is left before the answer, or when no page is open, as the request of a page that is gone. To ask the server for a Flight response yourself, use `handleRequest()`.
- Only `fetch` reaches the app. `XMLHttpRequest`, which axios uses by default, `EventSource`, `navigator.sendBeacon()` and an `<img>` with a route handler's URL go to the dev server.
- Opening or leaving a page waits for a request that the server has not answered yet, also one of `handleRequest()`, for five seconds at most. A request that never answers makes every leave that long, and gives a warning.
- In watch mode, a file that shapes a route and that is added while Vitest runs is not seen until Vitest starts again: a new page, `layout`, `loading`, `error`, `not-found` or `default`. Next's route loader keeps a directory's files for as long as the process lives.
- A worker starts slowly, because it loads Next's runtime for three layers before its first test. With as many workers as cores, that first test can time out. `playground/nextjs-notes-demo` sets `maxWorkers: 4` for that.
